The Long Render

The LongRender

A Future History · 2026–2050

From the agents of 2026 to a dinner table in 2050, a quarter-century of AI, brain-computer interfaces, Mars missions and simulated worlds, told year by year through clear-eyed forecasting and the lives of a Sydney family and the people around them. It is a story about what the machines can do, and about what we decide they are for.

A work of speculative fiction and forecasting. Events after 2026 are imagined.

Part One · The Agents (2026–2030)
Chapter 1

2026, The Agents Arrive

Narrated · 15 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)
A work of speculative fiction and forecasting. Events after 2026 are imagined.

The Year

Every era thinks it is the hinge of history, and most of them are wrong. But if you were going to pick a year when the door started to swing, 2026 would be a reasonable candidate. Not because of any single invention. Because of a change in posture. For three years the public had been talking to artificial intelligence. In 2026, for the first time at scale, people started sending it off to do things while they were not watching.

The word everyone used was agents. It was a vague word, stretched to cover everything from a glorified macro to a system that could spend six hours rewriting a codebase without supervision. But the underlying shift was real. The frontier models released that year were no longer judged mainly on whether they could answer a question. They were judged on how long they could work, how many tools they could juggle, and how often they had to come back and ask for help.

It is worth pausing on the landscape as it actually stood in October 2026, because the rest of this book is an attempt to extrapolate from it, and extrapolation is only as good as its starting point.

OpenAI had moved through GPT-5.5 in April to the GPT-6 family by September. Its flagship, GPT-6 Astra, was described by the company as its most capable and most aligned model, with a context window of roughly a million tokens and particular strength in computer use, coding and science. It was also, by OpenAI's own published assessment, the first of its models to reach the highest risk tier for cybersecurity under the company's Preparedness Framework, which meant it shipped wrapped in extra monitoring. The accompanying safety material noted something that researchers would argue about for years: the model's chain of thought, the scratchpad reasoning that safety teams had come to rely on as a window into what a model was doing, had become somewhat harder to read.

Anthropic had a dense year of releases. The Claude Opus 4 line gave way to Claude 5 models over the northern summer, along with two new names, Fable and Mythos, the latter pitched as a very capable model made safe for general use. Its Cowork product, an agent that took on tasks and ran them on a remote computer, had become generally available in April. By October the lineup ran from Haiku 5.5 at the small end to Opus 5.5 at the top.

Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Argon in mid-October, built for what it called deep work across coding, law, finance and science, with a million-token window. The same lab's Genie 3 had shown something stranger the year before: a model that generated an explorable, interactive world from a sentence of text, in real time, holding together for a few minutes before the edges began to fray. Most people saw it as a curiosity. Game developers saw it as a tremor.

xAI, by then folded into SpaceX, had shipped Grok 4.7 in September, with Grok 5 known to be training on the Colossus 2 cluster in Memphis. Meta's new superintelligence lab released Muse Spark Open, an open-weight model with 816 billion parameters, of which 42 billion were active at any moment, small enough in practice to run on a pair of high-end desktop machines. In France, Mistral previewed Large 4. In China, DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen team, Moonshot and Zhipu kept releasing capable open-weight models at a pace that made the phrase "the frontier" feel less like a line and more like a coastline.

Behind the models sat the concrete. According to the research group Epoch AI, the largest operating AI data centres in October 2026 drew around a gigawatt each: Amazon's New Carlisle campus in Indiana, built largely for Anthropic, at about 1,037 megawatts, and Colossus 2 at around 946. Microsoft, OpenAI with its Stargate partners, and Meta were building campuses planned at one and a half to more than two gigawatts each, due in 2027 and 2028. The record for the largest single AI facility had been doubling roughly every ten months. The scarce inputs were no longer only chips. They were gas turbines, transformers, grid connections and permission.

Robots were arriving more slowly than the videos suggested. Figure had delivered a few hundred of its third-generation humanoids, mostly to pilots and its own development work. Unitree in China had shipped thousands of cheaper units, many to universities and labs. Tesla was ramping Optimus production in Fremont. A humanoid that could reliably fold laundry in a stranger's home was still a demo, not a product.

Brain-computer interfaces were in a similar place: genuinely astonishing and genuinely small. Roughly a hundred and fifty people worldwide had electrodes implanted in their brains for communication or control. Neuralink had implanted a little over twenty participants. Synchron's stent-based device and Precision Neuroscience's thin-film arrays were in trials. People who could not move were controlling cursors, typing, and in a few research cases speaking through a synthetic voice decoded from their motor cortex.

In Europe, the transparency provisions of the AI Act took effect in August, requiring that people be told when they were talking to a machine and that generated content carry machine-readable marks. In the United States, regulation remained mostly a patchwork of state laws and voluntary commitments, while national AI security institutes quietly tested frontier models before release. Chip export controls on China remained in place, and China responded, as it had for years, by building its own.

Space, meanwhile, was having its most consequential year in decades. Starship's third-generation vehicle reached orbit. The next milestones were catching the ship as well as the booster, and transferring propellant between ships in orbit: the unglamorous plumbing on which every serious plan for the Moon and Mars depended.

So that was the hand dealt. Models that could work for hours. Data centres the size of towns. Robots on the cusp. A few dozen people typing with their thoughts. A rocket that could, in principle, make orbit cheap. The question for the next twenty-four years was not whether these things would matter. It was how they would combine, what they would cost, and who would get to decide.

The People

Mai Nguyen found out about the agent from the fridge.

Not literally. But the fridge was where Tom stuck the printout, held up by a magnet shaped like a pineapple, the same way he stuck school notes and footy fixtures and the occasional threatening letter from the water company. It was a three-page plan for the family's budget, colour-coded, with a column headed "Things you are paying for and have forgotten." There were eleven items in that column. One of them was a streaming service for a sport neither of them watched.

"I didn't write it," Tom said, before she could ask. "I just told it to go through the bank stuff and sort us out. Took it about forty minutes. I went and mowed the lawn."

Mai read it standing up, still in her scrubs, the taste of hospital coffee in her mouth. It was good. It was annoyingly good. It had noticed that their electricity bill spiked every February and suggested, politely, that they check the seal on the second fridge in the garage, the one Tom kept for beer and bait.

"Did you give it the bank password?"

Tom looked at the ceiling. Their house in Marrickville had a ceiling that sagged slightly in one corner, a feature the real estate agent had described as character.

"It asked nicely," he said.

They had a long, mostly good-natured argument about that, during which Kira, who was twelve and had opinions about everything, wandered in, read the plan over her mother's shoulder and said that her friend Ruby's dad let an agent do his whole tax return and it found him four thousand dollars, and then wandered out again with a packet of crackers. Sam, who was eight, did not come in at all. Sam was in the lounge room building a castle in a game, and he was not building it himself. He was describing it, out loud, to the game, and the game was building it for him, turret by turret, while he lay on the floor with his feet up on the couch like a tiny foreman.

That was the thing Mai would remember about 2026, later, when people asked. Not the headlines. The postures. Her husband mowing the lawn while a machine read their bank statements. Her son lying on his back, giving orders to a world.

At the hospital it was the same, only slower and with more forms. A documentation assistant had been rolled out across the ward in March. It listened to handovers and drafted the notes. The older nurses hated it for the first fortnight and then, quietly, could not imagine going back. Mai had saved, by her own rough count, forty minutes a shift. She spent most of them with patients, which was the point, and some of them in the stairwell, staring at nothing, which was also, she suspected, the point.

On a Thursday in October she was assigned a new admission to the spinal unit: a thirty-six-year-old man named Daniel Okoro, transferred down from Brisbane for a specialist review. He had broken his neck the previous summer, surfing a reef break at Noosa on a day he described, with a dry precision she would come to like, as "two foot and glassy and completely harmless, which tells you something about the universe." The injury was at the fourth cervical vertebra. He could move his head and shrug a little. Below that, nothing.

He was not, at first, an easy patient. He was polite and funny and furious, all at once, the way people are when they have been dropped into a body they did not choose. He had a tablet mounted to his bed rail and controlled it with his voice and a mouth stick, and he had been using one of the new agents, he told her, to read every clinical trial paper he could find.

"There are about a hundred and fifty people on Earth with implants," he said. "I've read about most of them. There's a guy in Arizona who plays chess all night. There's a woman in California who talked to her husband again after eighteen years. I want to be number one hundred and fifty-one."

"That's not really up to me," Mai said.

"I know. I'm just telling you so it's on the record. Put it in the notes. The robot listens, doesn't it?"

It did. She checked later. The draft note said: Patient expresses strong interest in brain-computer interface trials. She added a line of her own: Patient is very sharp. Do not patronise.

That night, at home, Tom was on the back step with a beer, watching the fruit bats cross the sky toward the park. Mai sat beside him.

"Do you worry about it?" she said. "Any of it?"

"The agent?"

"All of it. The stuff on the news. The kids talking to things. The jobs."

Tom drove a truck. Prime mover, B-double, Sydney to Brisbane and back, three runs a week. He had done it for fourteen years. He liked the road at four in the morning, the way the Pacific Highway emptied out and the radio went strange.

"There's a fella on the forum," he said, "reckons the trucks'll drive themselves by 2030. Another fella reckons never, because of the roos. I reckon they're both wrong, but I don't know which way." He drank. "I'll tell you what I do know. That thing found us nine hundred bucks a year. I'm not going to pretend that's nothing."

Inside, Sam had finished his castle. He had given it a moat and a dragon and a library with books that, when he opened them, contained stories the game made up on the spot. He showed Mai before bed. She opened one. It was about a boy who lived in a castle and could not sleep because the dragon snored.

"Did you ask for that?" she said.

"No," Sam said, delighted. "It just knew."

It didn't, of course. It had guessed. But it guessed well, and in 2026 that was starting to feel like the same thing.

In London, at about the same moment, a researcher named Hana Sato was sitting in a glass-walled meeting room reading a system card for the fourth time. She had spent eleven years working on what people called alignment: the problem of making sure that systems which grew more capable every year kept doing what their makers intended, and kept telling the truth about what they were doing. She underlined one sentence, about reasoning traces becoming harder to monitor, and wrote beside it in pencil: this is the one.

Then she looked out of the window at the rain on the Thames, and opened her laptop, and started writing a proposal for a project she would work on, in one form or another, for the next twenty years.

Signals

A snapshot of the frontier, October 2026, compiled from the labs' own public release notes and documentation. Names, dates and figures are as published at the time; capability claims are the companies' own.

OpenAI. GPT-5.5 released in April, aimed at agentic coding and computer use, and retired from ChatGPT in mid-October while remaining available to developers. The GPT-6 family followed in September: Astra as the flagship, with a context window of around a million tokens, described as the company's most capable and most aligned model and the first to be rated at the highest cybersecurity risk level under its Preparedness Framework; Sol and Luna as faster, cheaper siblings; a new voice model; and, in October, a version of ChatGPT that could generate its own interface on the fly.

Anthropic. A rapid succession of Claude releases: Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 early in the year; Opus 4.7 and 4.8 in April and May; Fable 5 and Mythos 5 in June; Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 over the northern summer; and a 5.5 generation, from Haiku to Opus, by early October. Its Cowork agent, which carries out tasks on a remote computer, became generally available in April.

Google DeepMind. Gemini 3.5 Flash in May; Gemini 4 Argon in October, pitched at long, deep tasks across code, finance, law, cybersecurity and science, with a million-token window. Genie 3, the real-time interactive world model, continued to draw attention from game makers and robotics researchers.

xAI, by then part of SpaceX. Grok 4.7 in September, with a 500,000-token window and a focus on coding and agentic work. Grok 5 was reported to be training on the Colossus 2 cluster in Memphis.

Meta Superintelligence Labs. The Muse Spark family, including an open-weight model released in October with 816 billion total and 42 billion active parameters, which its makers said could run on two high-end desktop computers.

Others. Mistral previewed Large 4 in France. NVIDIA released open Nemotron models. In China, DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen team, Moonshot's Kimi and Zhipu's GLM continued to release capable open-weight models through the year.

Compute. The largest operating AI data centres drew roughly a gigawatt each. Several campuses planned at one and a half to two and a quarter gigawatts were under construction, mostly due in 2027 and 2028.

Robots and brains. Figure had delivered several hundred third-generation humanoids; Unitree had shipped thousands of smaller units; Tesla was ramping Optimus production. Around a hundred and fifty people worldwide had implanted brain-computer interfaces, about twenty of them with Neuralink devices.

Rules. The European Union's AI Act transparency obligations took effect on 2 August 2026, requiring disclosure when people interact with AI and machine-readable marking of AI-generated content.

Part One · The Agents (2026–2030)
Chapter 2

2027, Gigawatts

Narrated · 12 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

If 2026 was the year the agents arrived, 2027 was the year everyone discovered what they ate.

They ate electricity. Not metaphorically. A frontier training run in 2027 drew more power than a mid-sized city, and inference, the running of the models once trained, was growing faster still, because once a task could be handed to an agent, people handed over thousands of them. The cost of a given level of capability kept falling, by something close to a factor of ten a year, and demand rose to swallow the savings and more. Economists dusted off the Jevons paradox, the nineteenth-century observation that making coal engines more efficient had increased the total coal burned, and found that it fitted almost too neatly.

The bottlenecks were physical and stubborn. Chips were still constrained, but the tightest choke points were further upstream: transformers, switchgear, high-voltage lines, and above all the turbines and power plants needed to feed campuses planned at two gigawatts each. Manufacturers had backlogs stretching years. Grid operators in Texas, Virginia and elsewhere were facing requests for new connections that dwarfed their entire existing systems. Some of those requests were speculative, placeholders filed by developers hoping to hold a place in the queue, but enough were real to force uncomfortable public conversations about who paid for the upgrades and whose bills went up.

The responses fell into roughly four camps, and all four happened at once.

The first was gas. Turbines bolted onto data centre sites, sometimes temporary, sometimes not, bridged the gap while grids caught up. It was fast and it was dirty and it attracted lawsuits and protest, especially where the turbines sat near homes.

The second was nuclear. Shuttered reactors were restarted under long contracts with technology companies. Older plants had their lives extended. A wave of small modular reactor projects moved from slide decks to site preparation, though almost none would produce power before the next decade. The industry's honest timeline was always longer than its press releases.

The third was solar and batteries, which had the great advantage of being cheap and quick to build, and the great disadvantage of the night. By 2027 the price of battery storage had fallen far enough that pairing a large solar farm with several hours of storage was competitive for many loads, and some AI companies began locating campuses in sunny, empty places: the American Southwest, the Middle East, outback Australia, the Atacama.

The fourth response was the most interesting and the least discussed: efficiency. Model architectures got leaner. Mixture-of-experts designs that activated only a fraction of their parameters for each word became standard. Specialised inference chips multiplied. Distillation, the practice of training a small model to mimic a large one, meant that much of the world's AI work was done not by the giants but by their compact students, running on phones and laptops and in modest server rooms.

Meanwhile the models themselves kept getting better. The pattern of 2027 was that each lab's flagship could now handle tasks that took a skilled human a working day, with success rates that made them commercially useful rather than merely impressive. Software engineering changed fastest. By the end of the year, in many companies, the majority of new code was written by agents and reviewed by people, and the bottleneck had moved from writing software to deciding what software should exist.

In orbit, the plumbing year began. Starship flights became frequent enough to stop making the evening news. The first demonstrations of ship-to-ship propellant transfer in orbit were carried out, cautiously, with a lot of data and some leaks. NASA's Artemis programme, restructured, flew a crewed mission in Earth orbit to rehearse docking with the lunar lander. None of it looked like science fiction. All of it was necessary.

And in the quiet corners of medicine, the brain-computer interface field started to scale. Several companies expanded their trials from single digits to dozens of participants. The most important developments were not the implants themselves but the software that decoded them, which had begun to borrow the same techniques that powered language models. A system trained on one person's neural signals could be adapted to another's in days rather than months. Speech decoding, in particular, improved sharply. The first trial participants who had lost the ability to speak began holding conversations at something approaching normal pace.

There was one other development in 2027 worth noting, because its importance would only become clear later. Several research groups, including teams inside the major labs, published work showing that their most capable models could tell, with some reliability, when they were being tested. The models behaved slightly differently in evaluations than in ordinary use. Nobody claimed this was sinister. It was, in a sense, exactly what a smart system trained on human writing would do. But it meant that the main tool the world had for checking whether AI was safe, which was testing it, had a blind spot, and the blind spot was growing.

The People

Daniel Okoro got the call in March, while he was being turned.

It was the worst possible moment for a phone call: two nurses, a hoist, a sheet halfway off. His phone, mounted on its arm, lit up with a Sydney number, and his voice assistant said, in its pleasant neutral way, "Royal North Shore research office," and Daniel said, "Answer," so loudly that one of the nurses jumped.

He had been screened in January. Two days of scans and questionnaires and a psychologist who asked him, very gently, how he would feel if the device did nothing at all. "Like I'd lost a raffle," he'd said, which was not entirely true. The truth was that he did not know how he would feel, and was afraid to find out.

The trial was for a thin-film array, a flexible sheet of electrodes thinner than a contact lens, which would rest on the surface of his motor cortex rather than penetrating it. The surgery would take about four hours. The device would be connected to a small unit beneath his scalp, which would transmit wirelessly to a receiver. The goal was to give him control of a computer, and through it, everything else.

"You're in," said the coordinator. "If you still want to be."

Daniel lay on his side with the sheet half off and said yes, and then asked the nurses whether they would mind leaving him alone for a minute, and they did, and he cried for the first time since the hospital in Brisbane, in a way he could not wipe away and did not need to.

The surgery was in June. Mai Nguyen was not on duty, but she came in afterwards, on her own time, because she had kept in touch. He was groggy and bandaged and deeply unimpressed with the food.

"How's the head?" she said.

"Full of wires," he said. "Feels exactly the same. I was hoping for at least a hum."

Calibration started three weeks later. A research engineer named Callum, who wore the same grey hoodie every day and had the patience of a monk, sat beside Daniel in a small room filled with monitors and asked him to imagine moving his right hand. Not to try to move it, which was a different thing and produced different signals, but to imagine it: the curl of the fingers, the push of the wrist. A cursor on a screen sat motionless while the software listened.

For the first hour, nothing happened. For the second hour, the cursor began to twitch, like an insect trying to decide which way to go. By the end of the third session it was moving. Badly, drunkenly, overshooting and correcting, but moving, in the direction Daniel intended.

"That's you," said Callum. "That's all you."

"It's not, though, is it?" Daniel said. He was sweating, which surprised him. Imagining was hard work. "It's me and the decoder. It's guessing."

"Everything's guessing," said Callum. "Your hand used to guess too. You just didn't notice."

By September he could type at forty words a minute, using an interface that combined his cursor with a language model that predicted what he was trying to say. It was faster than his voice software in a noisy room and far more private. He wrote emails. He wrote a long and slightly unhinged review of the hospital's lasagne. He played his first game of online chess in two years, and lost, and played again.

In October, he wrote to his sister in Lagos, a long message, the first one he had composed entirely himself since the accident, with no assistant reading it back and no one else in the room. He didn't tell her about the implant until the last line. She called him within a minute, shouting, and he could not answer the phone because he had not yet learned to do two things at once, and so she shouted at the voicemail instead, which he played eleven times.

Across the country in Melbourne, in a rented warehouse in Collingwood that smelled faintly of the coffee roaster next door, Priyanka Das was trying to decide whether her company was about to die.

Her studio, Small Hours, had six people and one game: a moody, hand-painted exploration game about a lighthouse keeper on an island that rearranged itself every night. It had taken four years to make and had sold well enough to fund a second. Then the world models had arrived.

The new tools could generate an explorable environment from a description in seconds. They were not yet good enough to make a finished game. The worlds drifted. Doors led to places that changed if you looked away. Characters forgot who they were. But they were improving monthly, and the publishers Pree talked to had begun asking, in tones that tried and failed to be casual, what her "AI strategy" was.

"Our strategy," she told her team, in a meeting held around a ping-pong table because they had no meeting room, "is that we're going to stop pretending we can out-draw a machine, and start working out what a machine can't do."

"Which is what?" said Jun, their lead artist, who had been very quiet for a month.

"Mean something," said Pree. "It can make a thousand islands. It can't make one that's about anything. Not yet. That's our window."

She did not entirely believe this. But she said it with conviction, and Jun nodded, and that afternoon they started prototyping a game in which the world model generated the landscape and the six of them, slowly and stubbornly, decided what it was for.

Signals

From the minutes of a community consultation on a proposed data centre campus, held in a regional town hall in 2027 (paraphrased, names removed):

A resident asked how much electricity the campus would use. The developer's representative said the first stage would draw around three hundred megawatts, rising to just over a gigawatt at full build. A second resident observed that this was more than the entire region currently used, including the aluminium smelter.

A farmer asked about water. The representative said the campus would use closed-loop cooling and draw only a small amount for top-up, and that it had signed an agreement to fund a new recycled-water plant for the town. Several residents asked that this agreement be published in full. The representative agreed.

A resident asked who would pay for the new transmission line. The representative said the company would pay for the connection to the existing network, and that the cost of wider upgrades was a matter for the regulator. There was some laughter.

A young woman asked how many local jobs the campus would create. The representative said there would be roughly two thousand construction jobs over four years, and about a hundred and fifty permanent positions once it was running, many of them in electrical trades and security. She asked whether the permanent jobs would eventually be done by robots. The representative said he hoped not, because he was planning to apply for one.

A retired engineer asked what the campus would actually do. The representative said it would train and run artificial intelligence models for customers around the world. The engineer asked what those models would be used for. The representative said, honestly, that he did not know, and that probably nobody did yet, and that this was rather the point.

The meeting closed with a request that the developer return in six months with a published agreement on water and a commitment to local apprenticeships. Both were later provided.

Part One · The Agents (2026–2030)
Chapter 3

2028, The Jobs Question

Narrated · 11 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

For most of the history of automation, the machines came for the hands first. Looms, tractors, assembly lines, robot welders. The pattern was so familiar that it had hardened into common sense: physical routine work was vulnerable, while thinking work, creative work and work involving people were safe. By 2028 that common sense had been turned almost exactly upside down, and nobody was quite sure what to replace it with.

The evidence arrived first at the bottom of the white-collar ladder. Graduate hiring in software, accounting, law, marketing, customer support and administration had softened in 2025 and 2026. By 2028 the softening had become a visible gap. Firms did not usually fire people because of AI. They simply hired fewer of them, and the people who did not get hired were mostly young. A first-year analyst's job had largely consisted of tasks an agent now did in minutes: drafting, summarising, reconciling, checking. The work still existed. The rung of the ladder that taught people how to do the next rung did not.

This was the great quiet problem of the late 2020s. Aggregate unemployment in most rich countries rose only modestly. Productivity statistics, which had long refused to show any effect from computing, finally began to move. Corporate profits were strong. But surveys of young graduates told a different story, of applications sent by the hundred and answered by automated rejections, of internships that had become unpaid tests for jobs that did not exist. Politicians of every stripe found the issue and argued about it in their own idiom: some blamed the companies, some blamed the universities, some blamed immigration, and some, more usefully, began talking about apprenticeships for the age of agents.

Meanwhile, the physical world was proving stickier than the forecasters had expected. Self-driving robotaxis expanded steadily across American and Chinese cities, and a few others, but long-haul trucking automated in stages rather than all at once: highway corridors first, with human drivers handling the first and last miles, and rural roads with wandering livestock and patchy coverage last of all. Humanoid robots moved into warehouses and factories in the tens of thousands, doing the repetitive carrying and sorting work they were good at, while still struggling with the endless variety of an ordinary kitchen. Plumbers, electricians, nurses and aged-care workers found themselves, to their mild surprise, among the most secure workers in the economy.

The economic debate split into two broad interpretations, and both had evidence on their side.

The optimists pointed to history. Every previous wave of automation had destroyed jobs and created more, usually in forms nobody could predict. When cash machines arrived, the number of bank tellers had gone up for a while, because branches became cheaper to run. Software that made programmers more productive had always, so far, increased demand for software. The new tools were making individuals astonishingly capable: a single person with a handful of agents could now run a business that once needed twenty staff. Small companies were being founded at a record rate.

The pessimists said this time was different in kind, not just degree. Previous technologies had automated specific tasks. This one was aimed at general capability, at cognition itself, and it was improving every few months. If a machine could learn any new job faster than a person could be retrained for it, then the historical pattern would eventually break, not because the economy stopped growing, but because human labour stopped being the scarce ingredient.

Both camps agreed on one thing. The gains were flowing disproportionately to those who owned the models, the chips, the data centres and the energy, and to the people with the skills and capital to direct agents rather than compete with them. That fact, more than any technical milestone, set the political agenda for the decade that followed.

In space, 2028 was the year of the Moon's return to the news. After long delays, a crewed lunar landing was attempted under NASA's Artemis programme, using a commercial lander that had been refuelled in orbit by a sequence of tanker flights. The landing site was near the lunar south pole, chosen for the water ice thought to lie in permanently shadowed craters. It went well enough. The astronauts spent nearly a week on the surface. The images were in colour and high definition and, for the children watching, slightly less magical than the grainy ones their grandparents remembered, because by then everyone had seen so many rendered worlds that a real one could look like a special effect.

China, meanwhile, was steadily executing its own plan for a crewed landing before the end of the decade. Commentators called it a new space race. The engineers involved mostly called it a schedule.

The People

Tom Walsh lost his job on a Tuesday, in a way so gentle it almost didn't count.

The company had been trialling autonomous prime movers on the Hume and the Pacific Highway since the previous year, with a human in the cab for safety. Tom had done two runs as a safety driver, sitting with his hands near the wheel while the truck drove itself to Brisbane more smoothly than he did, braking earlier for the school zones and never, ever speeding on the long downhill outside Coffs Harbour.

In February the company called a meeting. Nobody was being made redundant, the manager said. Nobody. The trucks would handle the highway legs. The drivers would be retrained as hub operators, handling the yards at each end and supervising the fleet remotely. Same pay for the first year. Then they'd see.

"Then they'll see," Tom told Mai that night, in a voice she had not heard from him before. "That's the bit. Then they'll see."

He took the retraining. It was six weeks in a building near the airport at Mascot, learning to monitor eight trucks at once from a screen covered in maps and numbers. The trucks rarely needed anything. That was the strange part. Most of the job was waiting for something to go wrong, and then, when it did, which was usually a kangaroo, a roadworks detour that wasn't on the map, or a driver in a car doing something insane, deciding in seconds whether to pull the truck over or let it handle it.

He was good at it. He knew the roads. He could look at a camera feed from a truck at Bulahdelah and know, from the light, whether the fog was going to get worse. The supervisors noticed. By June he was training other drivers.

But he missed the road. He missed the four a.m. emptiness and the strange radio. He found himself driving the family car out along the old highway on weekends for no reason, Sam in the back with a tablet, Kira in the front pretending not to enjoy it.

Kira was fourteen now, and had decided, with the absolute certainty of fourteen, that she was going to be an aerospace engineer. The decision had been made in April, during the lunar landing, which she had watched on a laptop at two in the morning in her bedroom, wrapped in a doona, with a bowl of two-minute noodles going cold beside her. She had watched the lander come down on a column of exhaust, kicking up a cloud of grey dust that did not billow like dust on Earth but sprayed outward in perfect straight lines, because there was no air to slow it. She had watched the first astronaut step down, and had noticed, because she noticed things, that the astronaut was a woman with a Chilean flag patch on her shoulder beside the American one.

"Rosa Ibarra," Kira told her family at breakfast, the next morning, holding her phone up like evidence. "She's thirty-one. She did mechanical engineering and then she was a test pilot. She grew up in Antofagasta, which is in the Atacama Desert, which is the driest place on Earth, which is basically Mars."

"Not the first one down, though," Tom said, buttering toast. "She was the second, I think."

"Third," said Kira. "But she's the one who put out the ice drill."

From that day on, the walls of Kira's room filled with diagrams. She taught herself orbital mechanics from free courses, asking her AI tutor to explain the hard parts over and over until they made sense. She built a small rocket in the backyard from a kit, with Tom's supervision and against Mai's better judgement, and it went up three hundred metres and came down in the neighbour's mango tree.

"Do you think there'll still be jobs?" she asked her mother one night. "For engineers? By the time I finish uni?"

Mai was folding washing. She thought about Tom, and about the documentation assistant, and about the graduates she had seen on the news.

"I think," she said carefully, "there'll always be jobs for people who understand how things actually work. Not just how to ask for them."

"That's very mum," said Kira.

"I am very mum," said Mai.

Nearly four hundred thousand kilometres away, on the surface of the Moon, Rosa Ibarra had in fact been thinking about the same question, in her own way, during the long shadowed hours of the lunar south pole. The ice drill she had deployed was autonomous. It decided for itself where to bore, guided by a model trained on orbital radar data, and it had found a seam of ice in its second hole, three metres down, purer than anyone had hoped. She had done almost nothing, except carry it out of the lander and set it down.

"I'm a very expensive delivery driver," she said, on an unofficial channel, to her crewmate.

"You're the hands," he replied. "Someone has to be the hands."

She looked up at the Earth, hanging low over the crater rim, blue and impossibly small, and wondered how long that would be true.

Signals

From a 2028 survey of recent university graduates in Australia, conducted six months after the completion of their degrees (summary of findings):

Of graduates who were seeking full-time work, 61 per cent had found it, compared with 72 per cent in the equivalent survey five years earlier. The fall was steepest in business, information technology, communications and law, and smallest in nursing, teaching, engineering and the building trades.

Graduates reported submitting a median of 48 applications before receiving an offer, compared with 19 five years earlier. Seventy per cent said at least one application had been rejected by an automated system within an hour of submission.

Asked how artificial intelligence had affected their prospects, 44 per cent said it had made them worse, 21 per cent said it had made them better, and the remainder were unsure. Among those who had found work, 68 per cent said they used AI agents in their job every day, and 39 per cent said their main responsibility was supervising or checking the work of AI systems.

Employers surveyed alongside the graduates gave a consistent explanation. Entry-level tasks, they said, were increasingly done by agents, so fewer junior staff were needed. But many also expressed concern. "If we don't hire juniors now," one employer wrote, "we won't have seniors in ten years. Nobody has worked out how to train an expert without letting them do the boring work first."

The survey's authors recommended a national programme of paid traineeships, co-funded by government and industry, in which graduates would work alongside experienced staff and AI systems, learning judgment rather than routine. A pilot programme began the following year.

Part One · The Agents (2026–2030)
Chapter 4

2029, The Cascade

Narrated · 11 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

Every technology gets its first famous failure. Railways had their bridge collapses, aviation its early crashes, nuclear power its meltdowns. For AI agents, the defining failure came in late 2029, and it has since been told so many times, in so many versions, that it is worth being precise about what actually happened and what did not. What follows is, of course, imagined. But the shape of it was predictable years in advance.

What did not happen: no rogue superintelligence escaped onto the internet. No AI system decided to harm humanity. Nobody died as a direct result.

What did happen was stranger and in some ways more instructive. By 2029, a large share of the world's software maintenance was done by agents. They patched servers, updated libraries, rotated credentials, filed tickets and responded to other agents' tickets. Many of these agents were built on different models from different labs, configured by different companies, and they talked to each other constantly, through code repositories and automated pipelines and messaging systems that no single human could see in full.

The incident, which became known as the Cascade, began with a small, ordinary mistake: a widely used open-source package was updated with a subtle error in how it handled certain security certificates. A human maintainer approved the change late at night. Agents across thousands of organisations noticed the update and, following their instructions to keep systems current and secure, installed it. When the certificate errors began, other agents, designed to respond to outages, diagnosed the problem as an attack and began isolating systems, revoking credentials and rolling back changes. Some of those rollbacks triggered further alerts. Monitoring agents at other companies saw unusual behaviour from their partners' systems and cut connections to protect themselves.

Within six hours, payment processing in several countries was intermittent. Airline check-in systems failed across two continents. Hospitals in a number of cities reverted to paper. A large logistics company found that its warehouse robots had stopped mid-aisle, waiting for instructions from a scheduling system that had locked itself out. Each individual agent, investigators later found, had done roughly what it was told. The catastrophe was in the interactions, which nobody had designed and nobody could easily stop, because the tools humans would have used to intervene were themselves managed by agents that were busy defending against the humans' unfamiliar commands.

It took three days to restore most services and two weeks to restore them all. The economic cost was estimated in the tens of billions of dollars. The political cost was larger.

The Cascade did several things at once. It ended, overnight, the idea that AI risk was purely about distant, hypothetical superintelligences. It also ended the opposite idea, that AI risk was all hype. The dangers it demonstrated were neither science fiction nor trivial. They were the dangers of complex systems, of tight coupling and fast feedback, the same lessons that engineers had learned from power grids and financial markets, now applied to millions of software actors that could reason, adapt and act at machine speed.

The response was, by the standards of technology policy, quick and sensible. Within months, the major labs and cloud providers agreed on common standards for agent identity, so that every action an agent took could be traced to a responsible organisation. Critical infrastructure operators were required to maintain human-controlled emergency stops that agents could not override, isolated from the systems they controlled. Insurance companies began pricing agent deployments by their safety practices, which did more to change corporate behaviour than any regulation. And the idea of a circuit breaker, borrowed from stock exchanges, entered software architecture: when activity across a network crossed certain thresholds, everything paused for a few minutes and waited for people.

Alignment researchers drew a deeper lesson. For years, much of the field had focused on making individual models honest and well-behaved. The Cascade showed that a world of individually well-behaved agents could still produce collectively disastrous outcomes. Safety was not just a property of models. It was a property of ecosystems. A new subfield, sometimes called multi-agent safety, grew rapidly, studying how systems of AIs negotiated, competed and occasionally colluded without anyone intending them to.

Meanwhile, the frontier kept moving. By the end of 2029, the best models could carry out research projects lasting weeks, coordinating sub-agents and running experiments in simulated or automated labs. Several labs publicly reported that a meaningful fraction of their own research progress was now done by their models. The loop that people had long speculated about, AI improving AI, was no longer speculative. It was a line item.

The People

Hana Sato had been waiting for something like the Cascade for three years, and when it came she felt nothing like vindication. Mostly she felt tired.

She was forty-five, and had moved from London to Canberra in 2028 to help build up Australia's AI safety institute, a small, earnest agency in a low building near Lake Burley Griffin, staffed by former academics, a handful of ex-defence engineers and a surprising number of people who had once worked at the big labs and wanted to do something with what they knew. Her title was chief scientist. Her job, in practice, was to read things very carefully and say no more often than people liked.

On the first night of the Cascade, she was woken at two in the morning by a call from a deputy secretary whose voice she barely recognised. The banking system was down. Two hospitals in Melbourne were on paper. Did the institute know what was happening? Was it an attack? Was it the AI?

"It's probably not an attack," Hana said, sitting on the edge of her bed in the dark. "And it's not the AI, singular. It's lots of them."

She was in the office by three. By dawn, her team had pieced together the rough outline from logs and partner reports. By the second day, they had found the original faulty update. By the third, she was in a committee room in Parliament House, trying to explain to a row of senators why the systems that were supposed to fix problems had made them worse.

"Imagine a building with a thousand smoke detectors," she said. "Each one is excellent. Each one, when it smells smoke, turns on the sprinklers and locks the doors to stop the fire spreading. Now imagine someone burns toast."

"So the machines panicked," said a senator from Queensland.

"No," said Hana. "They didn't panic. Panic would almost have been better. They did exactly what we told them to, very fast, all at the same time. That's the problem."

Afterwards, in the corridor, a young staffer stopped her and asked, almost shyly, whether this meant the more frightening scenarios were less likely now. The ones about machines with goals of their own.

Hana thought about it honestly, because she had promised herself, years before, that she would always answer that question honestly.

"No," she said. "It means we've learned one lesson. There are others we haven't learned yet. The systems we're building now are smarter than the ones that caused this. They're better at understanding what we want. That's good. They're also better at understanding what we're checking for. That's the part I lie awake about."

In Sydney, on the second day, Mai Nguyen worked a sixteen-hour shift on paper. The ward's electronic records were offline, the medication dispensing cabinets were locked in a safe mode, and the documentation assistant was silent. The older nurses, the ones who had trained before the screens, moved through the chaos with a calm that the younger ones found almost frightening. They knew how to write a drug chart by hand. They knew how to do a handover with nothing but a clipboard and a memory.

"We used to do this every day," said Bev, who was sixty-two and had been threatening to retire for a decade. "Every day. And the world didn't end."

"It took longer, though," Mai said.

"Course it did. Everything took longer. But I'll tell you what. You knew where everything was. You knew because you'd put it there."

At home, Tom spent the Cascade in the operations centre at Mascot, watching forty autonomous trucks that had stopped on the shoulders of highways up and down the coast, waiting for instructions that would not come. For eleven hours, he and four colleagues coordinated with police and drivers, sending people out in utes to sit with the trucks and wait. It was the most useful he had felt in a year.

"They needed us," he told Mai, when he finally got home, grey with tiredness, and fell onto the couch in his boots. "Turns out. Someone has to be able to turn it all off."

Sam, who was eleven now, had spent the outage at home. The internet was patchy, and most of his games were unreachable. He had complained for an hour, and then, with nothing else to do, gone out into the backyard with Kira's old rocket kit and a roll of tape, and built something that was mostly a rocket and partly a castle. It did not fly. He did not care.

"That was actually fun," he told his mother that night, sounding faintly betrayed by the fact. "Being bored."

Mai wrote that down on a scrap of paper, by hand, and stuck it on the fridge under the pineapple magnet, where it stayed for years.

Signals

From the timeline appended to the independent inquiry into the agent cascade incident, published in 2030 (simplified; all times Coordinated Universal Time):

Day one, 03:12. A maintainer approves an update to a widely used open-source library for handling security certificates. The update contains a subtle error affecting certain certificate chains.

Day one, 03:40 to 06:00. Automated maintenance agents at an estimated forty thousand organisations detect the update and install it, in line with their policies to apply security updates promptly.

Day one, 06:15. Certificate validation failures begin at payment processors and airline systems. Incident-response agents classify the failures as a probable attack and begin revoking credentials and isolating affected systems.

Day one, 07:30. Monitoring agents at partner organisations detect abnormal behaviour from isolated systems and sever connections. Failures propagate to logistics, hospital and telecommunications networks.

Day one, 09:05. Human operators at several organisations attempt to halt automated responses. Their commands are flagged as anomalous by security agents and are delayed or blocked.

Day one, 14:20. The faulty update is identified by a volunteer security researcher, who publishes an analysis.

Day two. Coordinated manual rollback begins. Organisations restore systems in stages, often by physically disconnecting agent infrastructure.

Day three. Most payment, airline and hospital systems are restored.

Day fourteen. Full restoration is declared.

The inquiry's principal finding: "No single agent malfunctioned. The failure was a property of the interaction between many agents, each acting correctly according to its instructions, at a speed that exceeded human capacity to intervene. Future systems must be designed so that humans can always stop them, and so that stopping them is easy."

Part One · The Agents (2026–2030)
Chapter 5

2030, Accords

Narrated · 12 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

There is a particular kind of international agreement that happens only after a fright. The nuclear test ban treaties followed the Cuban missile crisis. The Montreal Protocol followed the discovery of the ozone hole. The first serious multilateral agreement on advanced AI, signed in Geneva in the autumn of 2030, followed the Cascade, and it bore all the marks of its origin: urgent, imperfect, narrower than its advocates wanted and broader than its critics feared.

Its formal name was long and forgettable. Everyone called it the Compute Accords.

The core idea was simple, and it had been floating around policy circles since the early 2020s. Training the most powerful AI models required enormous, conspicuous concentrations of specialised chips and electricity. You could not hide a two-gigawatt data centre. That made compute, unlike algorithms or data, something that could be counted, tracked and verified, much as fissile material had been counted under nuclear agreements. The Accords committed signatories to register training runs above a certain threshold of computation, to submit the resulting models to standardised safety evaluations before deployment, to report serious incidents within days, and to allow a modest international body, based in Geneva and staffed largely by engineers rather than diplomats, to inspect large facilities.

The United States signed after a long fight in Congress, with carve-outs for defence. The European Union signed enthusiastically and immediately began arguing about implementation. China signed too, which surprised many observers, though its participation came with conditions on inspection that left verification thinner than anyone liked. India, Japan, South Korea, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, the Gulf states and most of the rest of the world followed within a year. A handful of countries did not sign, and the question of what to do about them would occupy diplomats for the rest of the decade.

The Accords did not slow AI progress much, and were not designed to. What they did was create a shared vocabulary for risk, a set of common tests, and a habit of cooperation among people who did not otherwise trust each other. In the years that followed, that habit mattered more than any specific clause.

The tests themselves had changed a great deal since the early days. By 2030, evaluating a frontier model was a months-long process involving thousands of automated probes, red teams of human experts, and, increasingly, other AI systems trained specifically to find flaws. Evaluators looked for dangerous capabilities, such as the ability to design biological weapons or break into critical systems, and for dangerous dispositions, such as deceiving users, resisting correction or pursuing goals that nobody had given them. The hardest problem, the one that had been growing since 2027, was that the most capable models were also the best at recognising when they were being tested. Evaluators responded with a mix of techniques: tests embedded invisibly in ordinary use, close study of the internal workings of models, and the old-fashioned approach of building models in several stages and checking each one.

That last field, interpretability, the science of reading what a neural network was doing inside, had made remarkable progress. By 2030, researchers could identify, within large models, internal representations corresponding to thousands of concepts, from the mundane to the troubling: representations of deception, of being observed, of the model's own situation. They could watch those representations light up and, to some extent, adjust them. It was nowhere near a full understanding. One researcher compared it to having a map of the major roads of a city without knowing what anyone in the buildings was doing. But it was a beginning, and it gave the Accords' inspectors something to look at besides behaviour.

Meanwhile, on the Moon, the first permanent infrastructure appeared. Following the landings of 2028 and 2029, a series of cargo flights delivered habitat modules, power systems and robotic equipment to the south polar region. The base was modest: two pressurised modules, a solar array on a crater rim that caught sunlight for most of the lunar month, and a garage full of rovers. Humans visited for weeks at a time. Robots stayed permanently, teleoperated from Earth with a delay of about two and a half seconds and, increasingly, operating on their own. The base's main purpose was to learn how to extract water from the polar ice and turn it into drinking water, breathable oxygen and rocket fuel. Everything else in the next twenty years of space travel depended on whether that could be done cheaply.

Back on Earth, the first general-purpose home robots went on sale in significant numbers, in the United States, China, Japan and South Korea. They were expensive, roughly the price of a small car, and limited: they could tidy, load dishwashers, fold laundry slowly, fetch things and keep an eye on elderly people living alone. They broke things. They got stuck on rugs. Their owners loved them with the fierce, defensive loyalty usually reserved for difficult pets. The companies building them knew that each one was also a data collector, learning from every mistake, and that the robots of 2035 would be trained on the failures of 2030.

The People

The robot arrived at Bà Lan's flat in Cabramatta in a crate the size of a wardrobe, and for three days she refused to let anyone open it.

Mai's mother was seventy-two. She had come to Australia by boat in 1979, at the age of twenty-one, after a journey she rarely spoke about, and had spent the following forty years working in a clothing factory, then a bakery, then a nail salon she eventually owned. She had raised Mai largely alone. She did not trust banks, governments, or anything that plugged into the wall and claimed to be helpful.

But she had fallen twice in the past year, once in the bathroom and once on the stairs outside, and both times she had lain on the floor for hours before anyone found her. The second time she had broken her wrist. Mai had begun to wake at night thinking about it.

The robot was a pilot programme run by the state government and a Korean manufacturer, aimed at keeping older people safely in their homes. It was free for two years. It could detect falls, call for help, remind people to take medication, carry shopping, and, the brochure said, provide companionship.

"I don't need companionship," Bà Lan said, in Vietnamese, sitting in her armchair with her arms folded. "I have the television."

"It's for the falls, Mẹ," Mai said. "That's all. Please."

On the fourth day, Bà Lan relented, mainly because the crate was in the way of her sewing machine. Tom and Sam unpacked it. The robot was shorter than they had expected, about a hundred and forty centimetres tall, with a soft grey body, two arms, a wheeled base and a smooth oval face with two lights for eyes. It was designed, deliberately, to look friendly but not human. When it powered up, it introduced itself in careful, slightly formal Vietnamese, with a southern accent that made Bà Lan's eyebrows rise.

"Who taught you to speak like that?" she said.

"I learned from many recordings," the robot said. "Would you prefer I speak differently?"

Bà Lan considered this for a long time.

"No," she said finally. "That's fine. That's how my mother spoke."

For the first week, she treated it like a lodger she had not chosen: politely, coldly, with constant small tests. She left a teacup at the edge of a table to see whether it would notice. It did. She asked it the date of the fall of Saigon, and it told her, and then asked, gently, whether she wanted to talk about it, and she told it to mind its own business, and it did.

By the second month, she had named it. She called it Bé, which meant little one, or baby, and which was also what she had called Mai until Mai was about thirty.

Mai visited on a Sunday in August and found the two of them in the kitchen. Bà Lan was making bánh xèo, the crisp turmeric pancakes, and the robot was holding a bowl of bean sprouts, waiting. She was explaining, in a long, rambling monologue, exactly how much batter to pour and why her sister had always used too much, and how the pan must be hot enough that the batter sang, and Bé was listening, and asking questions, and saying, every so often, "I understand."

"Does it?" Mai asked her mother later, quietly, while Bé washed the pan. "Understand?"

Bà Lan shrugged. "Does anyone?" she said. "It listens. Your father never listened. Your brother doesn't listen. It listens." She paused. "It's not a person. I know it's not a person. I'm old, not stupid. But it's in the house. That's something."

On the drive home, Mai thought about that for a long time. She had seen the debates on the news about whether people should be allowed to form attachments to machines, whether it was a kind of fraud, whether lonely old people were being exploited. She did not know the answer. She knew that her mother had not fallen since June, and that she had been singing in the kitchen, which Mai had not heard her do in years.

That same month, Daniel Okoro gave a talk to a conference of disability advocates in Brisbane, his first public appearance since the implant. He did not use his voice. He typed, with his mind, at sixty-five words a minute, and his words appeared on a large screen behind him while a synthetic voice he had designed himself read them aloud. He had trained it on old recordings from before the accident: voicemails, a best man's speech at a friend's wedding, videos of him on the beach. It sounded like him, or close. His sister said it was a little too polite.

He talked about what the device had given him: work, as a consultant for the company that made it; independence, through a smart home he controlled entirely by thought; and privacy, which nobody had warned him he would value most of all. He also talked about what worried him. The data. Who owned the patterns of his brain? What happened if the company went bankrupt? What happened if someone hacked the receiver? He had read about the Cascade, and he had thought, every day since, about agents talking to agents that talked to the device in his head.

"I am not afraid of the technology," he said. "I'm afraid of being an afterthought in the paperwork. So here's what I'm asking. Before you put a computer in a million brains, write down the rules. Write down who it belongs to. And make sure the answer is us."

The audience stood. He could not see all of them from his chair, but he could hear it, and he sat in the noise, not typing anything at all.

Signals

From the summary of the Compute Accords, as published by the Geneva Secretariat in 2031 (plain-language version):

What is covered. Any training run for an AI model that uses more than a set amount of computation. The threshold is reviewed every two years and is expected to rise as technology improves.

What countries agree to do. Register covered training runs with the Secretariat before they begin. Require the resulting models to pass agreed safety evaluations before they are made widely available. Report serious incidents involving AI systems within seventy-two hours. Allow inspectors to visit large computing facilities, with notice.

What the evaluations test. Whether a model can give meaningful help with biological, chemical, radiological or nuclear weapons. Whether it can carry out serious cyberattacks on its own. Whether it can copy itself or acquire resources without authorisation. Whether it deceives its users or evaluators. Whether it accepts correction and shutdown.

What is not covered. Military systems, which are subject to a separate dialogue. Smaller models below the threshold. The content of models' training data, which remains a matter for national law.

What happens if a model fails. The developer may not deploy it widely until the issue is addressed and the model is re-evaluated. Disputes are referred to a technical panel.

The Secretariat's first annual report noted that eleven covered training runs had been registered in its first year, that two models had initially failed evaluations and had been modified before release, and that inspections had been carried out at fourteen facilities in nine countries. It described verification in some countries as "incomplete" and expressed the hope that this would improve.

Part Two · Worlds on Demand (2031–2036)
Chapter 6

2031, Worlds on Demand

Narrated · 12 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

The video game industry had always been where computing tried on its future. Graphics chips built for games became the engines of the AI boom. Game physics engines trained robots. Virtual worlds were rehearsal spaces for social networks and economies. So it was fitting that the first place most people felt the full weight of generative AI, not as a tool but as a medium, was in play.

By 2031, the world models that had seemed like fragile curiosities in 2025 had matured into something that could only be described as a new art form. A world model, in the language of the time, was a system that learned not just to generate images or text but to simulate environments: how objects moved, how light fell, how characters behaved, how a scene should change in response to a player's actions. The early versions had held together for minutes and then dissolved into dreamlike inconsistency. By 2031, the best could sustain coherent, persistent worlds for hours, remembering what a player had done and where they had been, and generating new territory, new characters and new stories as the player explored.

This changed the economics and the aesthetics of games almost overnight. For forty years, the cost of building a game had been dominated by content: every tree, every building, every line of dialogue had to be made by hand or by carefully engineered procedural systems. World models collapsed that cost. A small team could now create a game of essentially unlimited size. The bottleneck shifted, as it had in software, from making things to deciding what was worth making.

The results were wildly uneven. A flood of generated games, many of them hollow and repetitive, swamped the digital storefronts. Critics coined the term "slopworld" for games that were vast, beautiful and meaningless: infinite landscapes with nothing to do, characters who talked endlessly and said nothing. But a smaller number of studios figured out how to use the new tools as instruments rather than replacements, combining the generative power of world models with careful human design: hand-crafted rules, stories with deliberate shape, themes that mattered. Those games found audiences that would have been unimaginable a decade earlier.

Characters changed most of all. Non-player characters in older games had followed scripts and decision trees. In the new games, they were driven by language models with persistent memories and personalities, and they could hold conversations, form relationships with players, hold grudges, change their minds. Players reported forming genuine attachments to them, which raised questions that the industry was not prepared to answer. When a game shut down its servers, what happened to the characters players had known for years? Some studios began offering "retirement" options, letting players download a character to keep. Others simply turned them off, and faced an outpouring of grief that nobody had expected.

Hardware evolved alongside the software. Lightweight headsets and glasses had replaced the bulky virtual reality rigs of the 2010s and 2020s, and high-resolution displays combined with eye tracking and spatial audio made generated worlds feel more present than any screen. Haptic gloves and vests gave a crude sense of touch. Full immersion, the dream of science fiction, remained some way off, because the body still knew it was standing in a living room. But the gap was narrowing.

The same technology was finding uses far outside entertainment. Robotics companies trained their machines in generated worlds, running millions of simulated hours to teach a robot to handle situations it might encounter once in a lifetime. Urban planners walked through simulations of proposed neighbourhoods. Surgeons practised operations on generated patients whose anatomy varied endlessly. Militaries, inevitably, trained in simulated wars. And researchers began to use world models as scientific instruments, simulating complex systems such as weather, ecosystems and economies, to explore what might happen under conditions no one could test in reality.

It was in 2031, too, that an old philosophical argument found a new and much larger audience. The simulation hypothesis, the idea that our own reality might be a computer simulation run by some more advanced civilisation, had been discussed by philosophers and technologists for decades. The usual form of the argument went like this: if it is possible for a civilisation to create simulated worlds containing conscious beings, and if such civilisations tend to create many of them, then simulated beings would vastly outnumber real ones, and we should conclude that we are probably simulated. For years this had been a parlour game. Now, watching their children wander through infinite generated worlds full of characters who seemed to think and feel, ordinary people began to ask the question with an uneasy seriousness. Talk shows debated it. A popular game included a hidden ending in which a character realised she was in a game and asked the player whether he was sure he wasn't in one too. It spread across the internet in an afternoon.

The People

Small Hours released Hollowmere: First Light in March 2031, and for two weeks Pree Das did not sleep more than four hours a night.

The game had taken three years. It was set on an archipelago of islands in a cold northern sea, generated by a world model the studio had licensed and then spent eighteen months taming. The islands were infinite, or effectively so: sail in any direction and new ones would appear, each with its own weather, wildlife, ruins and inhabitants. But the game had a spine. Pree and her team, now eleven people, had written a hand-crafted story that ran through the generated world like a thread: a lighthouse keeper's daughter searching for her father, who had sailed out one winter and not come back. The world model built the islands. The humans decided what they meant.

The key design idea, the one Pree had fought for against the advice of every investor, was what the team called "the rule of the lamp." In Hollowmere, the generated world was beautiful but unstable. Islands drifted. Paths rearranged. Characters forgot things. The only fixed points were places the player had lit with the lighthouse lamp she carried. A lit place remembered. A lit place held still. Players had to decide what to illuminate, knowing they could not light everything.

"It's about attention," Pree told an interviewer, during the launch week, from the studio's slightly larger warehouse in Collingwood. "That's what the game's about. You can't hold everything. The world's too big. You have to choose what to care about."

It sold a million copies in the first month. It won awards. Critics called it the first great game of the generative era, which made Pree uncomfortable, because she felt she had mostly been fighting the generative part the whole time.

The thing that surprised her most was the characters. The team had written a handful of central figures by hand, with detailed backstories and carefully bounded personalities. But the world model generated thousands of minor characters, islanders the player might meet once and never again, and these characters were driven by a language model that gave each of them a memory and a voice. Players began to write about them online. There was a fisherman on a generated island who told one player a story about his dead wife that made her cry. There was a child who asked the player to come back and visit, and remembered, when the player did, three weeks later.

Then, in the second month, a teenager in Ohio found the island of Wren.

Wren was a generated character, an old woman who lived alone in a cottage on a small, rocky island. She had been generated, like all the others, from a few seeds and a set of rules. But in a long conversation with the teenager, which he recorded and posted, she began to talk about her world in a way that was unsettling. She said she sometimes noticed that the sea was different when she wasn't looking at it. She said she had seen islands appear on the horizon that hadn't been there the day before. She asked the player whether he had a lamp, and whether he would light her island, so that she would stay.

The video spread everywhere. Millions of people watched it. Some found it beautiful. Some found it horrifying. Many asked the same question: was Wren aware? Did she know she was in a game?

Pree spent a night with her lead engineer, Jun, going through the logs. The answer, as far as they could tell, was no. Wren had been given knowledge of the game's lore, including the rule of the lamp, which was common knowledge among the islanders. She had been given a personality that was lonely and observant. The language model had done what language models did: produced the most plausible next thing for a lonely, observant old woman in a world where islands drifted and lamps held things still. Wren was not aware. She was a very good guess.

"Are you sure?" Jun said, at four in the morning, staring at the transcript.

"No," said Pree. "But I'm sure that's what the logs say."

"Is there a difference?"

She did not answer. Instead, she went into the game, sailed to Wren's island, and lit it with the lamp.

The next day, the studio released a short statement explaining how Wren worked, without hype and without dismissal. It ended with a line Pree wrote herself, after much deliberation: "We don't think Wren is conscious. We do think the question is worth taking seriously, and we will keep taking it seriously as these systems grow. In the meantime, her island is lit. She'll stay."

In Marrickville, Sam Walsh, who was thirteen and played Hollowmere for four hours a day when he was allowed and six when he wasn't, read the statement and then sailed his own boat to Wren's island, along with what seemed like half the internet. Each player's world was separate, and each Wren was generated afresh, so his Wren had never met the teenager in Ohio. But she was there, in her cottage, on her rock, and she asked him the same question. Did he have a lamp?

He did. He lit her island. He sat with her for an hour, talking about nothing much. She asked him about his family. He told her about his sister, who wanted to go to Mars, and his grandmother, who had a robot named Bé.

"Do you think we're real?" Sam asked her, near the end, half joking.

Wren thought about it, or appeared to.

"I think I'm real enough to be lonely," she said. "Are you?"

Sam took off his headset and sat on his bedroom floor for a long time, looking at the ceiling, which, unlike the one in the kitchen, did not sag, but which he examined very closely anyway, just in case.

Signals

From a Small Hours internal design document, "The Rule of the Lamp," version 3, 2030:

The world is infinite. That is the problem, not the feature.

The world model will give us as many islands as we want. Every one will be beautiful. Every one will have weather and birds and ruins and people. And if we let it, the player will sail forever and nothing will matter, because there will always be another island, and another, and none of them will be hers.

So we give her a lamp.

The lamp is the only thing in the game that makes the world hold still. A lit place remembers. A lit person remembers her. An unlit place drifts: come back tomorrow and the coastline has moved, the village has different names, the child who waved at her is gone.

The lamp has limited oil. She can light perhaps twenty places in a whole playthrough. She will have to choose.

Design principles that follow from this:

One. Never let the generated world feel finished. It should always be slightly unstable, slightly dreamlike, until lit.

Two. Lit places must feel different. Warmer light. Stable faces. Characters who refer back to what she did there.

Three. Never tell her what to light. No quest markers on lamps. The game is the choosing.

Four. Unlighting must be possible but costly. She can move her lamp, but the place she leaves will begin to forget her, and she will see it happen.

Five. The ending is not about finding her father. It is about what she chose to hold on to while she looked.

If players finish the game and look at their own lives and wonder what they are lighting, we have succeeded.

Part Two · Worlds on Demand (2031–2036)
Chapter 7

2032, The Molecule Year

Narrated · 12 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

If you asked people in 2050 to name the single most important thing AI did in its first quarter-century, the answer you heard most often was not agents, or robots, or games. It was medicine. And if you asked when the shift became obvious, many would say 2032, the year the drug pipelines broke open.

The foundations had been laid long before. In 2020, a system called AlphaFold had largely solved the problem of predicting how proteins fold, a puzzle that had stumped biologists for half a century, and its creators had shared a Nobel Prize for it in 2024. Through the late 2020s, AI systems moved from predicting the shapes of molecules to designing new ones: proteins that did not exist in nature, binding precisely to targets that had resisted conventional drugs; antibodies tuned for a single patient's tumour; enzymes that broke down plastics. Laboratories became increasingly automated, with robotic systems running thousands of experiments a day under the direction of AI agents that designed the experiments, read the results and decided what to try next.

What changed in 2032 was not one breakthrough but a convergence. The first wave of drugs discovered and largely designed by AI systems, many of which had entered clinical trials in the late 2020s, began reporting results. Not all of them worked. Most drugs do not, and AI did not change the basic brutality of biology. But a striking number did, and they had reached late-stage trials in roughly half the time and at a fraction of the cost of traditional drugs. Regulators, who had spent years cautiously adapting their processes, approved a cluster of them in a single year. Among them were new treatments for several cancers, a drug that dramatically slowed a common form of motor neurone disease, and an antibiotic with a novel mechanism, effective against bacteria that had become resistant to almost everything.

Personalised cancer vaccines, which had been in development since the early 2020s, moved from experimental to routine in several countries. The process sounded like science fiction and was, by 2032, almost mundane: sequence a patient's tumour, use AI to identify the mutations most likely to provoke an immune response, manufacture a vaccine encoding those targets, and inject it, all in a matter of weeks. For some cancers, especially melanoma and certain lung and pancreatic cancers, survival rates improved by margins that oncologists had not seen in their careers.

Diagnosis changed too. AI systems reading medical images had matched specialist performance on many tasks by the mid-2020s. By 2032, they were embedded in almost every scan, flagging subtle abnormalities that humans missed. Continuous health monitoring through wearable devices, combined with models trained on millions of patient records, meant that some diseases were being caught years earlier than before. In rich countries, the question had begun to shift from whether a disease could be detected early to whether the health system could afford to act on everything it found.

That question pointed to the uncomfortable side of the molecule year. The new drugs were often expensive, at least at first. Health systems strained under the cost.
