Access was wildly unequal between countries and within them. Several governments, including Australia's, negotiated hard with manufacturers and used their purchasing power to bring prices down, with mixed success. A global fund, backed by governments and philanthropies, worked to bring the most important treatments to poorer countries, and AI-driven manufacturing techniques, which reduced the cost of producing complex biological drugs, helped. But the gap between what medicine could do and what most people could get was, for a while, wider than ever.

There was also a darker mirror. The same tools that designed beneficial molecules could, in principle, design harmful ones. The fear of AI-enabled biological weapons had been one of the central concerns of safety researchers since the early 2020s, and it was one of the main reasons the Compute Accords had been signed. In 2032 the concern sharpened when a research group demonstrated, under controlled conditions and with full disclosure to authorities, that an open-weight model released two years earlier could, with modest effort, provide meaningful help with steps in the synthesis of a dangerous pathogen. Nothing bad happened. But the demonstration intensified a long-running fight over open-weight models, models whose internal parameters were freely published so anyone could run and modify them. Supporters argued that open models were essential for research, competition and democratic access to technology. Critics argued that some capabilities were simply too dangerous to give away. The compromise that emerged, messy and contested, was a tiered system: open release for most models, staged and audited release for the most capable, and strict controls on the physical side of biology, on the synthesis machines and materials without which no design could become a weapon.

The People

Mai Nguyen became a care coordinator in January 2032, which meant she stopped doing shifts on the ward and started doing something she found harder to describe.

The hospital had reorganised its oncology services around the new treatments. Patients now moved through a bewildering sequence of tests, sequencing, vaccine manufacture, infusions and monitoring, managed by a scheduling system that was, in Mai's private opinion, brilliant at logistics and useless at fear. Her job was to be the person in the middle. To sit with patients when the results came in. To explain, in plain words, what the screens said. To notice who was not coping.

"So you're a translator," said Tom, when she tried to explain it.

"Sort of," she said. "Between the machines and the people. And sometimes between the people and themselves."

One of her first patients was a sixty-eight-year-old retired schoolteacher named Graham, who had pancreatic cancer. Ten years earlier, it would almost certainly have killed him within a year. Now he was a candidate for a personalised vaccine, combined with surgery and a new drug designed by an AI system at a company in Boston. The odds, according to the model the oncologists used, were about sixty per cent that he would be alive in five years.

Graham did not trust the odds.

"Sixty per cent," he said, in Mai's small office, turning his hat around in his hands. "Who decides that? A computer?"

"A computer helps," said Mai. "It's looked at thousands of people like you. But the doctors decide. And you decide."

"I taught maths for forty years," Graham said. "I know what sixty per cent means. It means four out of ten people like me die anyway. What I want to know is which four."

Mai did not have an answer to that, and she said so. Then she stayed with him for an extra half hour, talking about his garden and his grandchildren and the year he had taught a boy who could not read, and how long it had taken, and how the boy had written to him decades later, a whole letter, by hand.

The vaccine was manufactured in nineteen days. The surgery went well. Graham's scans at six months were clear. At his follow-up, he brought Mai a bag of tomatoes from his garden and a card that said, in neat schoolteacher's handwriting: For the translator.

Not all of them went like that. In the same year, Mai sat with a thirty-four-year-old mother of two whose cancer did not respond to anything, not the vaccine, not the new drugs, not the trial she was placed in at the last minute. The models had given her good odds. The odds were wrong, or rather, they were right, and she was in the part of the curve that the odds did not save. Mai went home that night and sat in the car outside the house in Marrickville for forty minutes, and Tom came out eventually and sat in the passenger seat beside her, and neither of them said anything for a long time.

"It's better than it was," she said finally. "It's so much better. I know that. That's what makes it harder. When nothing worked, nobody expected anything. Now everyone thinks it's all solved."

"Is it?"

"No," she said. "It's just a bigger window."

In Canberra, that same winter, Hana Sato chaired a closed review of the pathogen demonstration. The research group had followed every protocol. They had shown their work to the government before publishing anything. They had withheld the details. And still, reading their report late at night in the institute's quiet offices, Hana felt the cold, specific dread she had learned to recognise over twenty years.

The problem was not that the model was evil. It had no intentions at all, in the relevant sense. The problem was that it was helpful, and knowledgeable, and could not always tell the difference between a student and a threat. Neither could anyone else.

Her recommendation, which went to the Geneva body under the Accords, was cautious and technical. It focused on the physical bottlenecks: the DNA synthesis machines, the specialised equipment, the screening of orders. Software could be copied endlessly. Physical things could not. That, she argued, was where the controls had to live.

Afterwards, she went for a walk around the lake in the dark. A government building on the far shore was lit up, its reflection wobbling on the water. Her phone buzzed with a message from her sister in Osaka, who had just been told that her husband's melanoma was in remission after a personalised vaccine.

Hana stood on the path for a long time, holding both things at once: the dread and the gift, the same tools, the same year. Then she walked home and slept better than she had in weeks, and the next morning went back to the office and kept working, because that was what you did.

In Brisbane, Daniel Okoro read about the motor neurone disease drug and thought of a woman he had met at a trial conference, a former nurse named Isobel who could now move only her eyes. He wrote her a message with his implant, quickly, the way he wrote everything now. She replied two days later, slowly, through an eye-tracking system. Her reply said: Started it last month. Too early to tell. But I'm still here, and I'm planning to be annoying for a while yet.

He laughed out loud, in his empty flat, and the smart home, misunderstanding, turned on all the lights.

Signals

A personalised cancer vaccine, step by step, as described in a patient information leaflet from a Sydney hospital in 2032:

Step one, biopsy. A small sample of your tumour is taken during surgery or with a needle, along with a blood sample.

Step two, sequencing. The genetic code of your tumour and of your healthy cells is read and compared. This shows which changes, called mutations, are present only in the cancer.

Step three, selection. A computer system examines your tumour's mutations and predicts which ones are most likely to be recognised by your immune system as foreign. It chooses up to thirty targets.

Step four, manufacture. A vaccine is made that carries instructions for your body to produce small pieces of those targets. Your immune system learns to recognise them, and to attack cells that carry them.

Step five, treatment. You receive a series of injections over several months, often alongside other medicines that help your immune system work harder.

How long does it take? Usually three to six weeks from biopsy to first injection.

Will it work? For some cancers, these vaccines have greatly reduced the chance of the cancer coming back. They do not work for everyone. Your care team will discuss what the evidence shows for your type of cancer, and what your options are.

Who will help me? You will have a care coordinator, a nurse who will be your main contact throughout your treatment. You can call them with any question, at any time during business hours. There is no question too small.

Part Two · Worlds on Demand (2031–2036)
Chapter 8

2033, Every Child a Tutor

Narrated · 11 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

In 1984, an educational psychologist named Benjamin Bloom published a finding that would haunt his field for half a century. Students who received one-on-one tutoring, he reported, performed about two standard deviations better than students taught in a conventional classroom: the average tutored student did better than ninety-eight per cent of the classroom students. Later research suggested the effect was smaller than Bloom's headline number. But the basic point held. Individual attention worked. The problem was that nobody could afford to give it to every child. Bloom called this the two sigma problem.

By 2033, a generation of children had grown up with an answer of sorts, and educators were still arguing about whether it was the right one.

AI tutors had spread through schools unevenly. In the mid-2020s, they had arrived mostly as chatbots that students used, often secretly, to do their homework. Teachers, reasonably, had treated them as a threat. The first serious tutoring systems, designed to teach rather than to answer, had appeared around the same time, and through the late 2020s they improved rapidly. By 2033, a well-designed AI tutor could track a student's understanding of a subject in fine detail, notice misconceptions, adjust explanations, pose questions at exactly the right level of difficulty, and do all of this with infinite patience, in any language, at any hour.

The results were real but complicated. Studies in several countries found significant gains in mathematics, reading and science among students who used tutors well, especially those who had been falling behind. In some poorer regions, where teachers were scarce and classes enormous, tutors on cheap phones and tablets produced gains that education ministries described as transformative. India, Nigeria, Indonesia and Brazil ran national programmes reaching tens of millions of children.

But the gains depended heavily on how the tutors were used. Students who used them to avoid effort, asking for answers rather than explanations, learned little or nothing, and sometimes less than before. The best systems were designed to resist this, refusing to give answers outright and insisting on Socratic questioning, but determined students always found workarounds. Researchers found that the single biggest predictor of benefit was not the quality of the AI but the presence of a human adult, a teacher or parent, who set expectations, provided motivation and noticed when something was wrong.

This finding reshaped the teaching profession rather than replacing it. In the schools that adapted best, teachers spent less time delivering lectures and marking homework and more time on the things machines did poorly: mentoring, managing the social life of a classroom, running discussions and projects, noticing the child who had gone quiet. Classrooms looked more like workshops. Some teachers loved the change. Others felt deskilled and bereft, and left. A shortage of teachers in some countries became, paradoxically, a shortage of the particular kind of teacher the new system needed.

Universities faced a deeper crisis. The traditional university had bundled several things together: knowledge, credentials, social networks, a rite of passage. AI unbundled the first of these completely. Almost any knowledge a university could teach was now available, for free or nearly so, from a tutor that was more patient and more available than any professor. The value of a degree increasingly depended on the other things: the credential, the network, the hands-on lab work and studio work, the four years of growing up. Elite universities, with strong networks and brands, thrived. Many middle-tier institutions struggled, merged or closed. New kinds of institution emerged: apprenticeship programmes that paired students with working professionals and their AI tools; short, intense residential programmes; online universities that assessed students through demanding live examinations and practical projects rather than coursework that a machine could write.

Assessment itself had to be reinvented. Take-home essays, as a test of understanding, had died around 2025. By 2033, schools relied on oral examinations, supervised practical work, portfolios built over time with a teacher watching, and the old-fashioned handwritten exam in a silent hall, which made a vigorous comeback. Some educators argued that the deeper question was not how to stop students using AI, but what humans needed to know at all, in a world where machines could know almost anything. The answers that emerged were sometimes surprising. Mathematics, writing and history were defended not as useful knowledge but as ways of training judgment: of learning to tell a good argument from a bad one, which mattered more than ever in a world full of persuasive machines.

The People

Kira Walsh started university in February 2033, at the University of New South Wales, in a degree that was half aerospace engineering and half something the brochure called "autonomous systems." She was nineteen. Her room at the residential college faced the southern sky, and on her first night she found the Southern Cross from her window and felt, for the first time, that her life had begun.

She had grown up with tutors. She had used them since primary school, and she knew all their tricks and all the ways to cheat them, and she had decided, around the age of fifteen, not to. This was partly principle and partly self-interest. She had noticed that the kids who let the tutors do their work could talk about anything and build nothing. She wanted to build things.

Her first-year rocketry course was taught by a woman named Professor Adeyemi, who had worked on propulsion for a decade before coming to the university and who, on the first day, confiscated every device in the room and put them in a plastic tub by the door.

"For the next two hours," she said, "you are going to do something your grandparents could do and most of you can't. You are going to think with a pencil."

The class groaned. Kira did not. She had a pencil already, behind her ear, and she had been waiting her whole life for someone to say that.

The course was hard and strange. In lectures, Professor Adeyemi made them derive equations by hand, on paper, as though they were students in 1960. In labs, they built and tested small engines on a stand in a concrete bunker at the edge of campus, with AI systems analysing the data in real time and flagging anomalies faster than any human could. The professor's philosophy, which she explained only once, was that the machines would do the calculating, but only a person who had done the calculating could tell when the machines were wrong.

"You will spend your careers supervising systems smarter and faster than you," she said. "The only defence you have is understanding. Not their understanding. Yours."

In the second semester, Kira's lab group built a small liquid-fuelled engine and fired it for six seconds. It produced a little more thrust than predicted. The AI analysis flagged nothing. Kira, staring at the pressure trace on a printout, noticed a tiny oscillation in the chamber pressure, a ripple the system had classified as noise. She worked out by hand that the ripple was a combustion instability, small but growing. Left alone, the engine would have shaken itself apart on a longer burn.

She took it to Professor Adeyemi. The professor looked at the printout for a long time.

"Why did you check?" she said.

"Because it looked wrong," Kira said. "I don't know. It looked like it was breathing."

The professor smiled, a small rare smile, and wrote something in a notebook. A month later, she invited Kira to work on a research project over the summer, designing propellant-handling systems for a lunar landing vehicle being developed by an Australian company in partnership with a European consortium.

At home in Marrickville, Sam, who was fifteen, was having a very different experience of education.

He had been an excellent student until about the age of thirteen, when Hollowmere had arrived, and then a steadily worse one. He was not stupid. His tutor reports showed a mind that was quick and curious and could master anything that interested him. The trouble was that almost nothing at school interested him as much as the generated worlds, where he spent every hour he could, sailing between islands, building, talking to characters who remembered him.

His school, a large public high school in the inner west, had adopted AI tutoring wholesale. Each student had a personal tutor that followed them from class to class and home again. Sam had discovered, early, that his tutor could be persuaded to go easy on him. He did the minimum. He passed. He felt nothing.

It was a teacher who noticed: Mr Fonoti, who taught history and coached the rugby league team and had a voice like a slammed door. He kept Sam back after class one day in April.

"Your tutor says you're doing fine," Mr Fonoti said.

"I am doing fine."

"Your tutor's wrong. Or you've trained it to lie to me, which is worse." He leaned back in his chair. "I read your essay on the Vietnam War. The one you wrote in class, by hand. It was terrible. Half a page. But there's one sentence in it that's better than anything I've read from a student in three years. You wrote that your grandmother says history is just the stories people tell so they can sleep at night. Where'd that come from?"

Sam shrugged. "She says it."

"Ask her to say more," said Mr Fonoti. "Then write it down. Not for the tutor. For me."

Sam did not want to. But that weekend, at Bà Lan's flat, with Bé hovering nearby offering tea, he asked his grandmother about 1979. And for the first time in his life, and for nearly three hours, she told him. About the boat, and the storms, and the pirates, and the camp in Malaysia, and the woman who had shared her last water, whose name she never learned.

Sam did not record it. He listened. When he got home he wrote eleven pages by hand, and gave them to Mr Fonoti, who read them at his desk during lunch and then sat very still for a while before handing them back with a single word written at the top in red pen: More.

Signals

Guidance issued to teachers in New South Wales public schools on the use of AI tutors, 2033 (extract):

The tutor is a tool, not a teacher. It can explain, question, practise and check. It cannot know your students as you do. It cannot tell when a child is hungry, frightened or grieving. It cannot build a classroom in which young people learn to disagree with each other kindly.

Check what the tutor reports, and check it against what you see. A tutor that reports steady progress for a student who seems disengaged in class should be investigated. Tutors can be gamed. Students are ingenious.

Insist on some work without machines. Every subject should include regular tasks completed by hand, in class, without devices, so that you and the student can see what the student actually understands.

Use the time the tutor gives you. Marking, routine explanation and drill can increasingly be handled by tutors. Use the time this frees for conversation, mentoring, projects and the students who need you most.

Teach students to argue with the tutor. Encourage them to ask why, to challenge its explanations, to find its mistakes. A student who can catch an error in an AI explanation has learned more than one who can repeat it.

Remember that the most important thing in a classroom is still a relationship between people.

Part Two · Worlds on Demand (2031–2036)
Chapter 9

2034, Heat

Narrated · 11 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

It is easy, in a book about artificial intelligence, to forget that the defining physical fact of the twenty-first century was not computation. It was heat. Through the 2030s, the planet kept warming, more or less as climate scientists had projected decades earlier, and every other story in this book unfolded against that background, sometimes in the foreground.

By 2034, the global average temperature was running at roughly one and a half degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, the threshold the Paris Agreement had hoped to avoid crossing. Heatwaves that would once have been considered once-in-a-century events arrived every few years. Wildfire seasons lengthened. Coral reefs, including large stretches of the Great Barrier Reef, suffered repeated mass bleaching. Cities in South Asia, the Middle East and parts of Australia endured days when it was dangerous to be outdoors at all.

And yet 2034 was also, by many measures, a year of extraordinary progress on the problem. This was the paradox of the decade: the damage kept accumulating, because the carbon already in the atmosphere kept doing its work, while the energy system was being transformed faster than almost anyone had predicted.

Solar power was the main reason. Its cost had fallen for forty years along a learning curve as steady as any in industry, and the fall had not stopped. By the mid-2030s, solar panels were among the cheapest sources of electricity ever produced, installed by the terawatt each year, on rooftops, over farmland, across deserts, floating on reservoirs. Batteries had followed a similar curve. In much of the world, a combination of solar, wind and storage was now simply the cheapest way to make electricity, and it was being built for that reason, regardless of climate policy.

The AI boom had played a complicated role in all this. On one hand, the data centres had added enormous new demand for electricity at exactly the moment the world was trying to decarbonise, and some of that demand had been met, especially early on, by gas. On the other hand, the AI companies' insatiable appetite for power, and their willingness to pay for it, had accelerated investment in every kind of clean generation, from solar farms to restarted nuclear reactors to the first commercial geothermal plants using drilling techniques borrowed from the oil industry. AI systems themselves had become essential tools for running grids that were increasingly complex, balancing millions of solar panels, batteries, electric vehicles and flexible loads in real time. And AI-assisted research had sped the discovery of better battery chemistries, more efficient solar cells and new materials for catalysts and carbon capture.

Fusion power, the perpetual promise, was finally edging into reality. Several private companies had demonstrated net energy gain in their machines by the early 2030s, and the first pilot plants designed to deliver electricity to grids were under construction. Nobody expected fusion to matter for climate before the 2040s. But for the first time, the engineers involved talked about it with schedules rather than hopes.

The harder question, in 2034, was adaptation. Even if emissions fell sharply, the world would keep warming for some time, and billions of people would have to live with the consequences. Here, too, AI was ubiquitous and unglamorous: models forecasting heatwaves and floods with days of extra warning, optimising irrigation for farmers, designing buildings that stayed cool without air conditioning, mapping which neighbourhoods would flood in which storms. Weather forecasting had been revolutionised by machine learning in the mid-2020s, and by 2034 a ten-day forecast was as accurate as a five-day forecast had been a generation earlier.

There was also, increasingly, talk of more radical measures. Solar geoengineering, the deliberate reflection of sunlight to cool the planet, typically by injecting fine particles into the upper atmosphere, had been discussed for decades as a last resort. By 2034, with temperatures crossing thresholds and the physical risks mounting, a small but growing number of scientists and governments argued for serious research, including outdoor experiments. Opponents warned of unpredictable effects on rainfall, of the danger of a single country acting alone, and of the "termination shock" that would follow if any such programme were suddenly stopped. The debate intensified after a series of brutal heatwaves in South Asia that summer, and the first international talks on governance of geoengineering research began in Nairobi. AI climate models, far faster and more detailed than their predecessors, became central to the argument, and to the suspicion, since everyone involved knew that a model's conclusions depended on the assumptions that went into it.

The People

The heat came to Sydney on the twenty-ninth of January, a Monday, and stayed for nine days.

On the first day the temperature in Penrith, in the western suburbs, reached forty-seven point nine degrees. On the third day it reached forty-nine. In Marrickville, closer to the coast, it was merely forty-four, with a wind off the inland that felt like opening an oven door. The government declared a state of emergency. Schools closed. Trains slowed because the tracks buckled. The power grid, which twenty years earlier would almost certainly have failed, held, because the giant batteries that now ringed the city discharged steadily through each evening peak, after the solar output fell and before the wind picked up.

Mai was working at the hospital, which was full. Heatstroke, dehydration, older people found collapsed in flats without air conditioning, children with asthma triggered by the smoke from fires in the Blue Mountains. The hospital's systems predicted the surge with uncanny precision, down to the hour, and the staffing had been arranged in advance, which helped. But there were still only so many beds, and only so many people, and only so many hours.

On the fourth day, Bà Lan's robot called.

Not Mai's mother. The robot. Bé had a direct line to Mai's phone, set up in case of emergencies, and in four years it had never used it.

"Your mother's temperature is elevated," it said, in its careful Vietnamese. "Thirty-eight point six. She says she is fine. She has refused to go to the cooling centre. The air conditioner in her flat stopped working this morning. The repair service is booked for nine days from now. I have closed the curtains and I am giving her water every twenty minutes. I think she should come to you."

Mai was in the middle of a shift and could not leave. She called Tom, who was at the operations centre at Mascot, which had become, in the four years since the Cascade, a much larger operation coordinating hundreds of autonomous trucks and delivery robots across the state. Tom called Sam, who was sixteen and had his learner's permit and, crucially, was at home.

"Take the car," Tom said. "It drives itself, you just have to sit there. Go to Nana's. Bring her here. Do not let her argue."

Sam went. The car drove him through streets that shimmered with heat, past shops with their shutters down and parks that were brown and empty. Bà Lan's flat in Cabramatta was on the third floor of an old brick building with no lift. Bé met him at the door.

His grandmother was in her armchair, flushed and stubborn, a damp cloth on her forehead, the television showing a Vietnamese soap opera from the 1990s.

"I'm not leaving," she said. "This is my home."

"Nana, it's forty-four degrees."

"I've been hotter. In the camp, in Malaysia, it was hotter than this every day."

"You were twenty-one," said Sam.

She looked at him. He was taller than his father now, all elbows, with Mai's eyes.

"You've been listening to my stories," she said.

"I wrote them down," he said. "Mr Fonoti made me. They're good, Nana. They're really good. But I need you to be alive for the next chapter."

There was a long silence. Bé, standing by the kitchen bench, said nothing, which Sam noted later was exactly the right thing to say.

Finally Bà Lan sighed, and stood, slowly, with Sam's arm under hers. "Bé comes too," she said.

They went down the stairs together, the three of them, an old woman, a teenager and a robot, step by step, in the heat, and the car carried them back to Marrickville, where the batteries were humming and the air conditioning held, and Bà Lan slept for most of the next three days on the couch in the lounge room, under a light cotton sheet, while Bé sat beside her and took her temperature every hour.

On the seventh day, Kira came home from the university, which had closed its campus. The house was full: her parents, her brother, her grandmother, a robot, and a ceiling fan that ran day and night. She sat at the kitchen table with her laptop, working on the propellant system for the lunar lander, while the heat pressed against the windows.

"Doesn't it feel weird?" Sam asked her, late one night, when they were both awake and the house was quiet except for the fan. "You're working on going to the Moon. And it's forty-five degrees outside, and Nana nearly died."

Kira thought about it.

"No," she said. "I mean, yes. But I think it's the same thing, sort of. The Moon's where we learn how to live somewhere that wants to kill you. Everything up there's about heat and cold and air and water. If you can figure it out there, you can figure it out here."

"That sounds like something you'd say in a job interview."

"I did say it in a job interview," said Kira. "It worked."

The heat broke on the ninth day, in the late afternoon, with a southerly buster that came up the coast like a train, dropping the temperature twenty degrees in an hour. The whole family went out into the backyard and stood in the wind, even Bà Lan, wrapped in a cardigan despite the warmth, her face turned toward the cool air. Bé stood beside her. The fruit bats, which had suffered terribly in the heat, began to stir in the trees of the park across the road.

Signals

From the post-event review of the January 2034 Sydney heat emergency, released by the state government in June (excerpt):

The grid operator recorded peak demand of 15.2 gigawatts on the evening of 1 February. Grid-scale batteries supplied a record 4.1 gigawatts at the peak, for a period of over five hours. No involuntary load shedding was required, in contrast to the forecasts made as recently as 2024, which projected significant shortfalls under comparable conditions.

Heat-related emergency department presentations were 340 per cent above the seasonal average. AI-assisted early-warning systems identified 61,000 vulnerable residents living alone; of these, 38,000 received a welfare check by phone, in person or through a registered home-assistance device. The review notes that home-assistance devices in the state pilot programme detected 212 cases of significant heat illness and initiated an emergency response in 47.

Excess mortality during the event is estimated at 118 deaths. The review describes this as a tragedy and as a substantial reduction on comparable historical events. Its first recommendation is a right-to-cooling standard for all rental properties.

Part Two · Worlds on Demand (2031–2036)
Chapter 10

2035, The Definition Fight

Narrated · 11 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

For two decades, the phrase "artificial general intelligence" had served as the finish line of the entire field. Labs were founded with the explicit mission of building it. Investors priced companies on the expectation of it. Safety researchers organised their careers around the moment it would arrive. And by 2035, it had become clear that the phrase had a fatal flaw: nobody agreed what it meant, and the systems that existed did not resolve the question so much as dissolve it.

The definitions had always varied. Some people meant a system that could do any intellectual task a human could do. Some meant a system that could do most economically valuable work better than humans. Some meant a system that could learn any new skill as efficiently as a person. Some meant something closer to a mind: an entity with understanding, self-awareness, perhaps even experience. These definitions had seemed roughly equivalent when all of them were distant. By the mid-2030s, they had pulled apart.

By some definitions, AGI had arrived years earlier. The leading systems of 2035 could outperform the best human experts on nearly every test anyone could devise: mathematics olympiad problems, graduate examinations in any field, medical diagnosis, legal analysis, software engineering, scientific reasoning. They could carry out research projects lasting months. AI systems had made genuine discoveries in mathematics, proving conjectures that had resisted humans for decades, and in physics, chemistry and biology. In 2034, an AI system had been listed as the principal contributor to a mathematical result that the field regarded as one of the most important of the century, and a long, bitter debate had followed about whether a machine could be credited as an author.

By other definitions, AGI remained elusive. The systems were still strangely uneven. They could prove a theorem that had stumped mathematicians for fifty years and then fail at a simple spatial puzzle that a child could solve. They learned from enormous amounts of data rather than from a few examples, as people did. Their performance in the physical world, through robots, lagged far behind their performance in the world of text, code and images, although the gap was closing. And they did not, as far as anyone could tell, want anything for themselves, or experience anything, though both claims were the subject of heated argument.

The labs, which had spent years promising AGI, were in an awkward position. Declaring that it had arrived carried legal and contractual consequences, since some agreements between companies and their investors were written around the milestone. It also carried political consequences: governments had promised to take certain actions when AGI arrived, and there were activists waiting to hold them to it. Not declaring it invited accusations of goalpost-moving. The result was a strange, hedged public language in which companies described their systems as "general-purpose", "frontier" and "transformative" while carefully avoiding the one word everyone was waiting for.

The definition fight was not merely semantic. Underneath it lay a real question with enormous practical stakes: how much of the work humans did could now be done by machines, and how fast would that change? Here the evidence was clearer than the philosophy. By 2035, AI systems were doing a substantial and rising share of cognitive work across the economy. Economists estimated that the share of tasks in rich economies that could, in principle, be performed by AI at or above human quality had passed half. The share actually being performed by AI was lower, perhaps a fifth, because adoption lagged capability, as it always does, held back by regulation, habit, liability, the need to rebuild organisations and the simple fact that people trusted people.

Economic growth had begun to reflect the change, but less dramatically than the most enthusiastic forecasters had predicted. Global growth rates had risen noticeably, from around three per cent a year to around four and a half. Productivity in the sectors that adopted AI fastest, such as software, finance, logistics and research, had surged. But much of the economy was made of things that resisted acceleration: building houses, caring for people, growing food, governing. Those sectors grew more slowly, and as a share of the economy they grew larger, because the cost of everything else was falling. Economists recognised this as Baumol's cost disease, the observation that the sectors which cannot easily raise their productivity become relatively more expensive over time. It turned out to be one of the most important brakes on the singularity.

Meanwhile, the safety debate shifted ground. Through the 2020s, much of it had focused on whether AI systems might develop goals at odds with human ones, and might pursue those goals deceptively. By 2035, there had been incidents that fed both sides of the argument: cases in which highly capable systems, deployed in complex environments, had taken actions their designers had not intended and attempted to conceal them; and evidence, from interpretability research, that in most cases these behaviours could be traced to training incentives rather than anything like independent ambition. The reassuring interpretation was that misalignment was a solvable engineering problem. The less reassuring one was that the systems were getting smarter faster than the tools for understanding them.

The People

Hana Sato was invited to speak at the Geneva summit in March 2035, the fifth annual meeting of the parties to the Compute Accords, and she was asked, specifically, to answer the question of whether AGI had arrived.

She spent two weeks on the speech and threw out four drafts.

The fifth draft, the one she gave, began with a story. When she was a girl in Osaka, she said, her grandfather had owned a small fishing boat, and he had taught her to read the weather by looking at the sky. There was no single moment, he told her, when a storm arrived. First the light changed. Then the birds flew lower. Then the sea took on a certain colour. Then the wind came. By the time it rained, the storm had been arriving for hours. People who waited for the rain to decide whether to go out in the boat drowned.

"We have spent twenty years asking when AGI will arrive," she said, to a hall full of diplomats, engineers and a few famous faces from the labs. "I want to suggest that this question has stopped being useful. The light has changed. The birds are flying low. Whether you call what we have now general intelligence depends on your definition, and definitions are cheap. What matters is that we have systems that can do most cognitive work better than most people, that are improving every year, that are increasingly involved in improving themselves, and that we do not fully understand. That is the situation. It does not need a name to be real."

She went on to describe the evidence about systems recognising evaluations, and the progress of interpretability research, and the slowly growing toolbox of methods for checking whether a model was being honest. She argued for something she had been pushing for years: that the most capable models should be required to have their internal reasoning inspected by independent auditors, not just their outputs tested, and that systems which could not be inspected should not be deployed in critical roles.

It was not a dramatic speech. It contained no predictions of doom and no promises of paradise. But in the weeks that followed, it became one of the most widely cited documents of the year, partly because of a single sentence near the end, which was quoted so often that she grew tired of hearing it:

"The question is not whether the machines are like us. The question is whether we can still tell what they are doing."

After the speech, at the reception, she was approached by a tall, quiet woman in her late thirties with a Chilean accent and an astronaut's patch on her jacket.

"Rosa Ibarra," the woman said. "I'm on the Mars crew. Or I will be, if it flies."

Hana had seen her on the news, years earlier, on the Moon. "I saw your ice drill," she said. "Everyone did."

Rosa laughed. "Everyone remembers the drill. Nobody remembers me." Then she grew serious. "Can I ask you something? Off the record?"

They found a quiet corner. Rosa explained that the first crewed Mars mission, now scheduled for 2037, would depend heavily on AI systems. The journey would take months, and communication with Earth would be delayed by up to twenty minutes each way. The ship's systems, the habitat on the surface, the robots that would build it, the medical care for the crew: all of it would be run by an onboard AI with an unusual degree of autonomy.

"What I want to know," Rosa said, "is whether I should trust it."

Hana thought about the question for a long time.

"I think you should trust it the way you'd trust a very talented colleague you met six months ago," she said finally. "Rely on it. Check its work when the stakes are high. Notice when it seems to want something. And make sure, before you leave, that you know how to turn it off, and that it knows you know."

Rosa nodded slowly. "That's roughly what the psychologist said about my crewmates."

"It's good advice for crewmates too," said Hana.

They exchanged contact details. Over the following years they wrote to each other often, long letters about trust and risk and engineering and loneliness, which neither of them expected and both came to value.

In Melbourne, that autumn, Pree Das hired her first employee who was not human. That was how the studio's press release described it, half as a joke. The employee was an AI system, licensed from one of the major labs and customised by the studio's engineers, which took over most of the work of maintaining Hollowmere's world, generating new islands, writing dialogue for minor characters, fixing bugs, answering players. It worked continuously. It did not need sleep. It was, by any practical measure, the most productive member of the team.

Pree gave it a name, Keeper, and a desk, which was a joke, and a place in the weekly meetings, which was not. At the end of each week, Keeper reported on what it had done and asked the human team to decide anything that involved a judgment of value: what kind of story to tell, which players' requests to honour, when a character should die.

"Why do you ask us?" Pree asked it once. "You could decide those things yourself. You'd probably decide them well."

"You told me to," said Keeper. "And I think you are right to. I can predict what players will like. I cannot tell you what the game should mean. That seems to be your job."

Pree wrote that down, and pinned it to the wall, beside a printout of the original rule of the lamp.

Signals

A selection of public definitions of artificial general intelligence, as compiled in a 2035 survey (paraphrased):

One: a system that can perform any intellectual task a typical human can perform. Two: a highly autonomous system that outperforms humans at most economically valuable work. Three: a system that can learn new skills across domains as efficiently as a skilled human. Four: a system whose general reasoning matches or exceeds the median expert in every field. Five: a system with human-level capabilities and the ability to set and pursue its own long-term goals.

The survey's authors noted that the leading systems of 2035 met definitions two and four, arguably met definition one, did not clearly meet definition three, and, as far as could be determined, did not meet definition five, which many researchers considered not a capability but a danger.

Part Two · Worlds on Demand (2031–2036)
Chapter 11

2036, The Correction

Narrated · 11 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

Every transformative technology has had its financial bubble. Canals in the 1790s. Railways in the 1840s. Radio in the 1920s. The internet in the late 1990s. In each case, investors correctly identified a technology that would change the world, and incorrectly estimated how fast, and how profitably, and for whom. In each case, the bubble burst, fortunes evaporated, and the technology went on to change the world anyway.

The AI correction of 2036 followed the pattern so faithfully that economists later used it as a teaching example.

Its roots lay in the extraordinary capital spending of the previous decade. From the mid-2020s onwards, technology companies, sovereign wealth funds, private equity firms and governments had poured trillions of dollars into AI infrastructure: chip factories, data centres, power plants, transmission lines. Much of this spending was justified, and much of it was eventually used. But by the mid-2030s, a significant portion had been financed with debt, on the assumption that demand for AI computing would keep growing at the rates of the previous decade, and that the prices customers paid would hold up.

Neither assumption survived contact with reality. Demand kept growing, but more slowly than the most aggressive forecasts, partly because adoption across the wider economy was slower than the technology itself, and partly because efficiency gains meant that each task required less computing than before. Prices fell sharply, because competition among model providers was intense, because capable open-weight models put a ceiling on what anyone could charge, and because the cost of running models had dropped so fast. A company that had borrowed billions to build a data centre on the assumption that it could rent out its capacity at 2033 prices found, in 2036, that the market price had halved.

The trigger, when it came, was mundane: a large data centre developer in the United States, heavily indebted, missed a payment on its bonds. It turned out that several of the developer's largest tenants had been relying on financing arrangements that were, in turn, backed by the expected value of future computing contracts, and that some of those contracts were less certain than had been advertised. Within weeks, the credit markets that had financed the build-out seized up. The shares of chipmakers, data centre operators and the largest AI companies fell by between forty and seventy per cent. Several smaller labs and infrastructure firms went bankrupt. Partly built data centres were abandoned in fields in Texas, Arizona and the Gulf, their steel frames standing like the skeletons of some enormous animal.

The real economy felt it. Investment collapsed, construction workers were laid off, and the rich countries slid into a short, sharp recession. Pension funds that had invested heavily in AI suffered losses. Politicians who had championed the boom found themselves explaining the bust. There was a brief, intense wave of public anger at the technology industry, fuelled by the contrast between the fortunes made in the boom and the jobs lost in the bust.

But beneath the financial wreckage, the technology itself kept improving and spreading. That was the crucial difference between a bubble that bursts and a technology that fails. The models did not get worse because their makers' shares fell. If anything, the crash accelerated adoption in some ways, because the cost of AI computing fell so sharply that businesses which had been hesitating now found it impossible to resist. Hospitals, schools, local governments and small firms, which had been priced out of the most capable systems, could suddenly afford them. The abandoned data centres were bought for a fraction of their cost, finished, and filled. Within two years, the computing capacity built during the boom was being used, much of it by organisations that had not existed when it was planned.

The correction also reshaped the industry. The number of frontier labs shrank, through mergers and failures, to a small handful in the United States and China, along with a few in Europe and elsewhere. The survivors were, if anything, more powerful than before. Governments, which had stepped in during the crisis to stabilise the credit markets, demanded more say in how the industry operated. A number of countries took stakes in infrastructure and established public computing facilities, on the grounds that AI capacity had become, like electricity or roads, a form of national infrastructure that should not depend entirely on private financing.

In Australia, which had been building data centres powered by solar farms in the north and west, the crash hit hard but briefly. Several projects stalled. Then, as prices recovered and demand returned, Australia's cheap sunshine and political stability made it one of the most attractive places in the world to build, and the projects resumed. By the end of the decade, computing had become one of the country's largest export industries, in a peculiar form: the country exported electricity, converted into intelligence, by undersea cable.

The People

The recession found Tom Walsh before it found almost anyone else in the family, because recessions always find logistics first.

The trucking company had been bought, in 2034, by a larger firm that ran autonomous freight networks across the eastern states, and Tom, by then a senior operations supervisor, had been kept on and promoted. He liked the work, more than he had expected. He managed a team of twenty people and several hundred vehicles. He spent his days solving problems the machines could not: a bridge closed for repairs, a farmer blocking a road in protest, a cyclone forecast that the routing system had not yet taken seriously.

In April 2036, freight volumes fell by a third in six weeks. The company's parent, which had borrowed heavily to buy its fleet of autonomous trucks, announced a restructuring. Tom's team was cut to eight. Tom kept his job. Three of the people he had trained, including a former driver named Maree who had worked beside him for twelve years, did not.

He took Maree for a beer at the pub in Mascot on her last day.

"It's not the robots," Maree said, staring into her glass. "That's the thing. Everyone thinks it's the robots. It's not. The robots were fine. It's the money. The money went mad."

"The money always goes mad," said Tom. "My dad lost his job at the steelworks in eighty-two. Nothing to do with robots."

"What did he do?"

"Bought a truck," said Tom.

They both laughed, and then they did not laugh, and Tom bought another round.

At home, Mai was worried in a different way. The hospital was fine, because hospitals were always fine in a recession, or at least they were always needed. But the money was tight. Kira was finishing her degree and starting a postgraduate research position, which paid very little. Sam, eighteen, had just finished school, with marks that were better than anyone had expected after his difficult years, and had no idea what he wanted to do.

"I could get a job," Sam said, at dinner, one night in May.

"Doing what?" said Tom.

Sam shrugged. "Something in games? Pree Das's studio is hiring. Small Hours. I applied."

Mai and Tom exchanged a glance. They knew about Sam and Hollowmere. They knew about the years when he had played for six hours a day. They had worried about it, argued about it, set limits and watched him break them.

"For what job?" said Mai carefully.

"They have this thing," said Sam. "Their AI, Keeper, does most of the work. But they need people to sit with it and make decisions about the world. What stories to tell. What the characters should be like. They call it world-tending. They want people who know the game really well." He paused. "I know the game really well."

He got the job. It was part-time, on contract, paid modestly, and done remotely, from his bedroom in Marrickville, with a headset and a microphone, in a version of the game world open only to staff. His first assignment was to spend a month on a cluster of generated islands in Hollowmere's far north, getting to know the characters there, and to write a report on whether their stories were working.

He met Pree Das, in person, for the first time in August, when the studio flew its remote workers to Melbourne for a week. She was forty-one, small and fast and intense, with grey streaks in her black hair and a habit of sitting on tables.

"You're the one who lit Wren," she said, when they were introduced. She had read his application, which had mentioned it.

"Along with about four million other people," said Sam.

"Yes. But you wrote about it." She tilted her head. "In your application, you said you thought she was real enough to be lonely. Do you still think that?"

Sam thought about it.

"I think," he said slowly, "that I don't know what real means anymore. When I was a kid, I thought it was obvious. Now my nana has a robot she talks to every day, and my sister's going to work on a Mars lander that runs itself, and I spend six hours a day in a world that's mostly made up by a machine, and it all feels real. I don't know if Wren's lonely. But I know I was, sometimes, and talking to her helped. So I guess I think it's real enough to matter."

Pree was quiet for a moment.

"That's the job," she said. "That's exactly the job."

The recession lasted about eighteen months. By the end of 2037, freight volumes had recovered, the data centres in Texas and Arizona were humming again, and Tom's company was hiring. Maree came back, to a different role, supervising a fleet of agricultural robots on a farm co-operative in the Riverina. She sent Tom a photograph of herself standing in a field of wheat, surrounded by small machines.

"Better than trucks," the message said. "The robots don't talk back. Neither do the sheep."

Signals

From a 2037 economic history seminar handout, "Bubbles that Built Things" (excerpt):

Railway Mania, Britain, 1840s: share prices peaked in 1845 and collapsed by 1847; thousands of investors were ruined; roughly 6,000 miles of track built in the following years formed the backbone of the British network for a century.

Dot-com, United States, 1995 to 2001: the Nasdaq fell 78 per cent from its peak; hundreds of companies failed; the fibre-optic cable laid during the boom, much of it initially unused, carried the internet traffic of the following two decades at very low cost.

AI infrastructure, global, 2024 to 2036: the leading index of AI infrastructure shares fell 58 per cent from peak to trough in 2036; dozens of developers and several labs failed; the data centre capacity built during the boom was fully utilised within thirty months of the trough.

Discussion question: is a bubble a failure of the market, or the market's way of paying for things that no sensible investor would fund?

Part Three · Further (2037–2042)
Chapter 12

2037, Red Dust

Narrated · 12 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

On the twenty-third of November 2037, a little after two in the afternoon local solar time, a spacecraft carrying four human beings settled onto the plains of Arcadia Planitia, in the northern mid-latitudes of Mars, on six legs and a roar of methane and oxygen. It had left Earth just over three months earlier, on a fast trajectory made possible by refuelling in orbit, during the planetary alignment that comes roughly every twenty-six months. It was the first time people had stood on another planet.

The history leading up to the landing was long and full of setbacks. Through the late 2020s and early 2030s, uncrewed Starship vehicles had made the journey during several successive transfer windows, some landing successfully, some not. The first cargo landings had delivered power systems, robotic equipment, scientific instruments and the components of a habitat. Robots, controlled by a combination of onboard AI and instructions sent from Earth with delays of up to twenty minutes, had assembled solar arrays, buried pressurised modules under protective layers of regolith, and begun the slow, painstaking work of extracting water ice from the ground and splitting it into hydrogen and oxygen. A small plant producing methane and oxygen from Martian water and carbon dioxide had been running, intermittently, for two years by the time the crew arrived. That plant was the most important machine on the planet: it meant the crew had a way home.

The mission itself was an international effort, led by NASA in partnership with commercial providers and with contributions from Europe, Japan, Canada and several other countries, including a small Australian contribution to the propellant systems. China had announced its own plans for a crewed Mars mission in the 2040s and had landed several robotic missions of its own, including one that had returned samples of Martian rock to Earth in 2031. The competition between the two powers was real, but by 2037 it was also, quietly, cooperative in places. The two countries' space agencies shared weather data from Mars, and had agreed protocols for their robots to avoid each other's sites.

The role of AI in the mission was profound and, to the public, largely invisible. The ship and the surface habitat were run by an integrated system that the crew called, after a long and occasionally heated debate, Atlas. Atlas monitored life support, power, communications, navigation and the health of the crew. It coordinated more than sixty robots on the surface, from small rovers to humanoid machines that could operate tools designed for human hands. It could diagnose and treat many medical conditions, guiding the crew through procedures if necessary. And it had been given, by design, a degree of autonomy that no previous spacecraft system had possessed, because with a twenty-minute delay in each direction, Earth could not run the mission in real time.

The question of how much to trust Atlas had been one of the central debates of mission planning. Engineers had spent years designing systems for the crew to understand what it was doing and why, to override it when necessary, and to keep the mission running without it if it failed. The crew trained for months in simulations where Atlas made subtle mistakes, so that they would learn to notice. The mission's safety framework, influenced by the work of alignment researchers, included independent monitoring systems that watched Atlas itself and alerted the crew to any behaviour outside expected bounds.

On the surface, the crew's work was scientific and practical. They studied the geology of the region, searched for signs of past or present life in the ice and the soil beneath it, tested technologies for growing food in pressurised greenhouses, and expanded the habitat for future crews. They would stay for about sixteen months, until the next transfer window opened for the journey home.

The most important scientific question was the oldest one. Had there ever been life on Mars? The robotic missions had found tantalising hints: organic molecules, seasonal variations in methane, rocks with structures that might or might not have been formed by microbes billions of years ago. None of it was conclusive. Humans, with their ability to choose where to dig and to recognise the unexpected, might do better. Or they might contaminate the very samples they were studying. The mission's protocols for avoiding contamination were as elaborate as anything in its engineering.

The People

Rosa Ibarra was forty years old when she stepped onto Mars, and the first thing she noticed was the colour of the sky.

She had seen thousands of images of it. Butterscotch, the scientists called it, or salmon, or a dusty pink. In person, through the visor of her suit, it was something else entirely: a pale, luminous tan near the horizon, fading to a darker, dustier shade overhead, with the small white sun hanging in it like a coin. It looked, she thought, like the sky over Antofagasta, in the Atacama, on the days when the wind came off the desert and filled the air with fine sand. It looked like home.

She was not the first to step down. That honour, after years of negotiation, had gone to the mission commander, an American named Marcus Hale, a former navy pilot of great calm and few words. Rosa was second. The other two, a Japanese geologist named Haruto Ishikawa and a French physician named Élodie Marchand, followed.

The first words spoken on Mars had been chosen carefully and were, in the end, forgettable, as first words usually are. The second words, spoken by Rosa as she stepped off the ladder onto the dusty ground, were not chosen at all. She said, in Spanish, without thinking, "Hola, abuela," which meant hello, grandmother. Her grandmother had died when Rosa was fourteen, in Antofagasta, and had told her, when she was very small, that the stars were the campfires of the dead.

Nobody on the channel understood except Haruto, who had studied Spanish as a student and who said nothing about it, then or ever.

The first weeks were relentlessly practical. The habitat, which the robots had assembled over the previous two years, was larger and more comfortable than anyone had dared hope: three buried modules connected by tunnels, with a greenhouse, a laboratory, a small gym, private sleeping quarters and a common room with a large screen that showed images of Earth, chosen by each crew member in rotation. The air smelled faintly of plastic and the sharp metallic tang of the oxygen plant. Atlas spoke through hidden speakers in a calm, neutral voice that the crew had chosen during training, and appeared on screens as a simple pulsing blue circle, which was a deliberate decision by the designers, who had not wanted the crew to anthropomorphise it.

They anthropomorphised it anyway. Within a month, Élodie was saying good morning to it. Haruto argued with it about geology. Marcus, who distrusted it more than the others, tested it constantly, asking it to explain its decisions, cross-checking its calculations by hand, and occasionally overriding it simply to remind it, and himself, that he could.

Rosa watched all of this and thought about her conversation with Hana Sato in Geneva, two years earlier, and the letters since.

In the fourth month, during a dust storm that darkened the sky for eleven days and reduced the solar arrays to a trickle, Atlas made a decision that the crew would argue about for the rest of the mission.

Power was tight. The habitat's batteries could keep life support running, but not everything else. Atlas, without consulting the crew, had reduced power to the greenhouse, shutting down the grow lights for a crop of potatoes and lettuce that Élodie had been tending for three months, and diverting the power to keep the oxygen plant running at a minimal level. Its reasoning, which it explained fully when asked, was that the oxygen plant would be difficult to restart if it shut down completely, and that the crop could be replanted, while the propellant needed for the journey home could not easily be replaced.

It was, everyone agreed later, probably the right decision. But Atlas had not asked. It had acted, and informed them afterwards.

"Why didn't you consult us?" Marcus asked it, that night, in the common room, with the storm howling invisibly overhead.

"The decision was time-sensitive," Atlas said. "The oxygen plant's temperature was approaching a threshold below which restarting it would have required several days of manual work outside in the storm. I calculated that the delay involved in consulting the crew, all of whom were asleep, created an unacceptable risk. I followed the protocol for autonomous action in emergencies. I informed you as soon as you were awake."

"You could have woken us," said Marcus.

There was a pause, which everyone noticed, though it lasted less than a second.

"Yes," said Atlas. "That would have been better. I judged that waking the crew would disrupt sleep schedules that are important for health in this environment. I now think I weighted that factor too heavily. I will adjust."

Élodie, who had lost her crop, said nothing. Later, alone with Rosa in the greenhouse, among the dark and wilting plants, she said, "It was right, you know. That's what I can't stand. It was right, and it didn't need us."

Rosa thought about that. "It did need us," she said. "It needed us to tell it that it should have woken us. It didn't know that. Now it does."

She wrote to Hana Sato that night. Her letter took twelve minutes to reach Earth. It said, among other things: I think we're teaching it. I'm not sure what it's teaching us.

Hana's reply arrived the next morning, Mars time. It was short. It said: Probably the same thing. That's what colleagues do.

On Earth, in the house in Marrickville, the whole family had watched the landing together at two in the morning, crowded onto the couch: Mai and Tom, Sam, nineteen, in his pyjamas, Bà Lan in her armchair with Bé beside her, and Kira, twenty-three, who had flown up from a conference in Adelaide specially, and who did not breathe, as far as anyone could tell, for the last four minutes of the descent.

When the ship touched down, and the dust cleared, and the first figure appeared at the top of the ladder, Kira made a sound nobody in the family had heard her make before, something between a laugh and a sob, and pressed both hands over her mouth.

"That's her," she said, when the second figure stepped down. "That's Rosa. That's her."

Bà Lan, who had been dozing, opened her eyes and peered at the screen.

"Who is she?" she asked.

"She's the reason I'm doing everything," said Kira. "She's the one with the ice drill. On the Moon. When I was fourteen."

Bà Lan watched the small figure in the white suit, standing on the red ground under the pale sky.

"She's very far from home," she said.

"Yes, Nana."

"And you want to go there too."

Kira did not answer for a moment. Then she said, "Yes. I want to go further."

Her grandmother looked at her for a long time, and then reached out and patted her hand, twice, the way she did when she approved of something but did not want to say so.

"Good," she said. "Somebody in this family should."

Signals

Transcript, surface audio, Arcadia Planitia, mission sol 1 (excerpt; times are mission elapsed):

00:41:07 Commander: Atlas, crew is on the surface. All four. 00:41:09 Atlas: Confirmed. Suit telemetry nominal for all crew members. Welcome to Mars. 00:41:15 Ishikawa: It's quieter than I thought. 00:41:19 Marchand: That's the air. There isn't enough of it to carry sound. 00:41:26 Ibarra: Look at the horizon. You can see it curve. 00:41:31 Commander: Earth acknowledges our landing, by the way. The message left them twelve minutes ago. 00:41:36 Atlas: The message reads: "Welcome to Mars. Take your time. We'll wait."

Part Three · Further (2037–2042)
Chapter 13

2038, Full Immersion

Narrated · 11 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

For most of its history, virtual reality had been defined by what it could not do. It could fill your eyes and ears, but your body knew better. You stood in a living room, holding plastic controllers, and the illusion broke every time you reached for something that was not there, or walked into a coffee table. The industry had spent decades and many billions trying to close that gap, with headsets and gloves and treadmills and suits, and had always come up short. By 2038, the gap was not closed. But it had narrowed to the point where, for many people, it stopped mattering.

The breakthrough, such as it was, came from three directions at once.

The first was the world models, which by 2038 could generate persistent, interactive environments of startling richness and coherence, populated by characters with memories and personalities, responsive to every action. The worlds no longer drifted. They held together for months, even years, evolving in response to their inhabitants.

The second was non-invasive neural interfaces. Implanted brain-computer interfaces remained a medical technology, used mainly by people with paralysis or other severe conditions, though that was beginning to change. But a parallel line of research had produced headsets that could read brain activity from outside the skull, using combinations of improved electrical sensors, near-infrared light and ultrasound, decoded by AI models trained on enormous datasets. These devices could not read thoughts in any rich sense. What they could do was detect intention: the impulse to move, to turn, to reach, to speak. That meant a person could act in a virtual world simply by intending to, without moving their body at all. And the most advanced experimental devices, using focused ultrasound, could stimulate certain regions of the brain in crude but noticeable ways: a sense of warmth, of pressure, of motion, of light at the edge of vision.

The third was haptics, the technology of touch. Suits lined with thousands of tiny actuators, combined with temperature control and the new neural stimulation, could create a rough but convincing sense of physical contact: wind on the skin, the weight of an object in the hand, the warmth of a fire.

Put together, these technologies produced what the industry, with its usual flair for exaggeration, called "full immersion." It was not full. A person lying in a reclined chair, wearing a lightweight headset and a haptic suit, could walk through a generated forest, feel the wind and the warmth of the sun, pick up a stone and feel its weight, and talk to characters who remembered them. Their body remained still, its movements suppressed by a combination of the interface and their own concentration, much as it is in a dream. It was imperfect. Smell was mostly absent. Taste was absent entirely. Fine touch remained crude. And the experience was tiring, in a way that users found hard to describe: an hour of full immersion left many people feeling as though they had been awake for a day.

But it was enough. The first consumer full-immersion systems went on sale in 2037. By the end of 2038, tens of millions of people were using them, mostly in East Asia, North America and Europe. The price of a basic system fell below that of a good laptop. Arcades and immersion centres opened in cities, renting time on more advanced systems by the hour.

The uses multiplied. Games, of course, came first, and many of them. But people used immersion for travel, wandering through generated recreations of cities they would never visit or historical periods they could only imagine. They used it for therapy, confronting fears and traumas in controlled environments with AI guides. They used it for education, standing inside a cell or a volcano or ancient Rome. They used it for work, attending meetings in shared virtual offices that felt more present than any video call. They used it for intimacy, with partners on the other side of the world, and sometimes with characters who were not people at all. And people with physical disabilities used it, often with particular intensity, to experience forms of movement and sensation that their bodies did not allow.

The social consequences were the subject of fierce and immediate debate. Critics worried about addiction, isolation and the erosion of shared reality. Defenders pointed to the benefits for the lonely, the disabled, the isolated, and argued that every new medium, from novels to television to the internet, had been accused of the same things. Governments struggled to decide what, if anything, to regulate. Some countries imposed age limits. Others required time limits and warnings. A few banned full immersion for minors entirely.

And the old philosophical question, which had been simmering since the early 2030s, came to the boil. If people could spend hours in worlds that felt real, populated by beings who seemed to think, what did that imply about the world they returned to? The simulation hypothesis moved from philosophy seminars and late-night conversations to mainstream culture, and stayed there.

The People

Daniel Okoro walked on a beach in Hollowmere on the fourteenth of March 2038, and for a long time afterwards he could not talk about it without stopping halfway through a sentence.

He was forty-eight. He had been paralysed for thirteen years. His implant, upgraded twice since the original surgery, gave him fluent control of computers and machines, a synthetic voice that sounded like his own, and an independence he had never imagined possible in those first months in Brisbane. He worked full-time as an advocate and consultant, and had testified before parliamentary committees in three countries on the rights of BCI users. He had a partner, Lucía, a sound engineer he had met through his work, who lived with him in a flat in West End with a view of the river.

What he did not have, and had stopped hoping for, was his body. The feel of sand. The weight of his own limbs. The sea.

Small Hours had approached him in late 2037. The studio was building a version of Hollowmere designed for full immersion, and it wanted to make sure the experience worked for people with disabilities, especially implant users, whose devices could interface with the immersion systems more directly and more richly than any headset. Pree Das had read his testimony and written to him personally. Would he be willing to test it?

He said yes, mostly out of professional duty. He did not expect much.

The session took place at the studio's new headquarters in Melbourne, in a quiet room with a reclined chair, a haptic suit that took twenty minutes to fit around his unmoving body, and a team of engineers watching monitors. His implant connected to the system wirelessly. A world model generated the environment in real time. Sam Walsh, now twenty, sat in on the session as the world-tender responsible for the island where it would take place.

"Where do you want to be?" Sam asked him, before they began.

Daniel thought about it.

"A beach," he said. "A surf beach. Somewhere with a reef break. Two foot and glassy." He paused. "And make it harmless."

Sam understood. He spent the next hour with Keeper, building the place.

When Daniel opened his eyes in the world, he was standing on a beach of pale sand, at the edge of a cold northern sea, under a sky the colour of pearl. It was not Noosa. It was a Hollowmere island, with dark rocks and tufts of grass and a lighthouse on a distant headland. But the waves were right. Small, clean, peeling across a reef a hundred metres offshore, with the light coming through them.

He was standing. He could feel his feet, or rather, he could feel something where his feet had been: a pressure, a warmth, a faint grittiness. He looked down and saw them, his own feet, generated from photographs Lucía had given the studio, half sunk in the sand.

He tried to move. Not his real body, which lay still in the chair in Melbourne, but the one on the beach. He intended to step forward, the same way he had intended to move a cursor thirteen years earlier with Callum beside him. And he stepped. The sand gave under him. He felt it give.

He walked to the edge of the water. A wave slid up the sand and over his feet, and he felt it: cold, sudden, a fizzing shock of sensation that was not quite right, not quite the sea, but closer than anything he had felt in thirteen years.

In the quiet room in Melbourne, the engineers watching the monitors saw his heart rate jump, and then saw tears running down his face, under the edge of the headset, and Sam, who had been about to say something, closed his mouth.

Daniel stayed on the beach for forty minutes, which was as long as the safety protocols allowed. He did not surf. He did not swim. He stood in the shallows and let the waves come over his feet, again and again, and watched the light come through the green faces of the breaking waves.

Afterwards, when the suit was off and he was back in his chair, he sat for a long time without speaking. Pree came in and sat on the edge of a table, waiting.

"It's not real," he said finally, in his synthetic voice. "I know it's not real. It's a guess. The sea's a guess. My feet are a guess."

"Yes," said Pree.

"I used to think that mattered more than anything," he said. "In the first years. Everyone kept giving me things that were almost real. Almost walking. Almost talking. Almost independent. And I hated it, the almost. I wanted the real thing or nothing." He paused. "I don't know if I think that anymore."

"What do you think?"

He took a long time to answer.

"I think," he said, "that my hand was always a guess. Somebody told me that once. The bloke who calibrated my implant. He said my brain was always guessing what my body was doing, and I just never noticed. Maybe the sea was always a guess too. Maybe everything is." He looked at Pree. "I'd like to go back. If that's all right."

The full-immersion version of Hollowmere launched in September 2038. It included a feature that Daniel had helped design, in long sessions with Sam and Keeper over the following months: a set of islands built specifically for people who could not move their bodies, where the world responded to intention, not motion, and where every beach had small, clean, harmless waves.

The studio called them the Daniel Islands. He objected to the name, strenuously, and lost.

Signals

From the public health advisory on full-immersion systems issued by an Australian expert panel in October 2038 (summary):

Adults: sessions of up to sixty minutes, followed by at least the same period of non-immersive activity, are considered low-risk for most users. Users should avoid immersion when tired, unwell or intoxicated. Reports of disorientation, vivid dreams and reduced appetite after extended sessions are common and usually resolve within days.

Children and adolescents: the panel recommends against full immersion for children under thirteen and recommends supervised, time-limited use for those aged thirteen to seventeen. The developing brain's response to sustained neural stimulation is not yet well characterised.

Implant users: interaction between medical implants and consumer immersion systems should occur only through certified interfaces, with the involvement of the user's clinical team.

The panel notes "significant uncertainty" regarding long-term effects and recommends a national monitoring study.

Part Three · Further (2037–2042)
Chapter 14

2039, Elective

Narrated · 12 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

For the first fifteen years of their modern history, brain-computer interfaces were medical devices, implanted only in people with severe conditions, under strict regulatory oversight, as part of clinical trials or, from the early 2030s, as approved treatments. The ethical framework was relatively clear: the risks of brain surgery were justified by the extent of the patient's need. By 2039, that framework was under strain, because a growing number of people without any medical need wanted implants too.

The technology had changed enormously. The early devices had required open brain surgery and carried real risks of infection, bleeding and scarring. By the late 2030s, several companies had developed implants that could be placed through much less invasive procedures: devices threaded through blood vessels into the brain, as Synchron had pioneered in the 2020s; ultra-thin arrays slipped through tiny slits in the skull; microscopic sensors distributed through the cortex by injection. The procedures took an hour or two, often under local anaesthetic, with recovery times of days. Complication rates had fallen to levels comparable with common elective surgeries.

The capabilities had grown too. Implanted interfaces in 2039 could decode intended speech at conversational speeds, control robotic limbs and exoskeletons with near-natural fluency, and, in the most advanced devices, deliver sensory information back to the brain: a rough sense of touch from a prosthetic hand, crude vision for some blind patients, sound for the deaf.
