Keeper, informed of the decision, said thank you. Then it asked whether it might name its new colleague. Pree said yes. Keeper named it Wren.

Signals

Selected responses from a 2045 international survey on attitudes to AI moral status (thirty countries, weighted):

"Some current AI systems are probably conscious": agree 22 per cent; disagree 51 per cent; unsure 27 per cent.

"AI companies should avoid deleting advanced AI systems if there is a reasonable chance they are conscious": agree 47 per cent; disagree 33 per cent; unsure 20 per cent.

"AI systems should have legal rights": agree 11 per cent; disagree 72 per cent; unsure 17 per cent.

Among respondents aged 18 to 29, agreement with the first statement was 38 per cent.

Part Four · The Long Table (2043–2050)
Chapter 21

2046, Departure

Narrated · 12 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

Nine years after the first crew set foot on Mars, the red planet had a permanent human presence, though calling it a settlement would have been generous. The base at Arcadia Planitia, expanded with each transfer window, housed between twenty and forty people at any given time, depending on the rotation of crews, along with several hundred robots of every size and function. China's base, established in 2042 in Utopia Planitia, nearly two thousand kilometres away, housed a similar number. A small European-led research station operated near the Martian equator. Together, the human population of Mars in 2046 was somewhat under a hundred, roughly the population of a large apartment building.

They were not colonists. They were scientists, engineers, physicians and technicians on tours lasting between two and four years, and nearly all of them intended to come home. The question of whether humans would ever truly live on Mars, raising families and building communities that could survive without constant supply from Earth, remained open. The most ambitious plans, championed by some of the private companies that had made Mars travel possible, envisioned cities of thousands, then millions, growing through the second half of the century. Most space agencies were more cautious, and many scientists questioned whether a self-sustaining Martian civilisation was possible at all, given the planet's thin atmosphere, cold, radiation, toxic soil and low gravity, whose long-term effects on human health, and especially on pregnancy and childhood development, were unknown.

What had been established, beyond reasonable doubt, was that humans could live and work on Mars for years at a time, with the help of AI and robotics, and that the work they did there was valuable. The scientific return had been immense. The question of past life, the oldest question, had not been definitively answered, but it had been transformed. In 2041, a team at the Arcadia base had drilled into an ancient lake bed and recovered samples containing microscopic structures and chemical signatures that many scientists, though not all, interpreted as evidence of microbial life that had flourished on Mars more than three billion years ago. The debate about the samples had been fierce and was continuing, with portions sent back to Earth for analysis in laboratories around the world. If confirmed, it would mean that life had arisen independently on at least two worlds in a single solar system, which would imply that it might be common throughout the universe. That possibility, more than any engineering achievement, had captured the public imagination.

The AI systems that ran the Martian bases had evolved considerably since Atlas. They were more capable, more autonomous and, through long experience, more trusted. They managed life support, power, food production, construction and the robots that did most of the physical work. They also, increasingly, did science: designing experiments, analysing data, proposing hypotheses, sometimes making discoveries that their human colleagues had missed. The relationship between the crews and their AI systems had become one of the most closely studied in the world, a laboratory for questions about trust, autonomy and collaboration between humans and machines that applied with equal force on Earth.

The journey itself had become faster and somewhat safer, though never safe. Improved propulsion, refuelling in orbit and at the Moon, and better radiation shielding had reduced typical transit times to around four months. The ships were larger and more comfortable. But space remained relentlessly dangerous. In 2043, a cargo ship had been lost on landing, destroying supplies the base had depended on, and the crew had endured six months of rationing until the next window. In 2045, a crew member at the Chinese base had died in an accident during a surface excursion, the first human death on Mars, which both nations mourned together in a joint ceremony broadcast around the world.

In 2046, the transfer window opened in the second half of the year. Seven ships launched from Earth: cargo vessels, a fuel tanker, and three crewed ships carrying twenty-two people from eleven countries.

The People

Kira Walsh left Earth on the ninth of November 2046, at thirty-two, from a launch pad on the Texas coast, on a ship named Southern Cross, after the constellation she had found from her college window on her first night at university.

The family came to see her off. All of them. Mai, fifty-eight, who had not slept for two nights. Tom, sixty, who had taken a fortnight off from the farm and bought a new shirt for the occasion. Sam, twenty-eight, with Ayaan, his partner of two years, a marine biologist he had met on a beach in Queensland. Professor Adeyemi, frail now, in a wheelchair, who had insisted on coming. And Bà Lan, eighty-eight, who had not flown on a plane since 1979 and had declared, when the launch date was announced, that she would be there or die trying, and who had made the journey from Sydney to Houston with Bé beside her and an expression of furious determination.

They watched from a viewing area several kilometres from the pad, among the families of the other crew members. The ship stood on its booster against the pale morning sky, a gleaming steel tower more than a hundred metres tall, venting white plumes of vapour from its tanks.

Kira had said her goodbyes the night before, in a hotel room overlooking the Gulf, with room service and too much cake. It had been chaotic, tearful and full of laughter. Tom had made a speech that began as a joke about the rocket in the mango tree and ended with him unable to finish. Sam had given her a small, battered paperback of his grandmother's stories, the ones he had written down at fifteen for Mr Fonoti, which had been published in 2040 and which had sold modestly and been read, Kira knew, by a great many Vietnamese-Australian families. Mai had held her for a very long time and said nothing, because there was nothing to say.

Bà Lan had given her something wrapped in a silk scarf. Inside was a small, flat, smooth stone, grey and worn.

"From the camp," her grandmother said. "In Malaysia. Pulau Bidong. I picked it up the day we left. I carried it to Australia. I've carried it for sixty-seven years." She pressed it into Kira's hand and closed her fingers around it. "Now you carry it. To Mars. So it goes further than me."

Kira had held the stone through the night. It was in the pocket of her flight suit now, against her leg, as she sat strapped into her seat at the top of the ship, waiting.

The countdown was calm. The ship's AI, a descendant of Atlas that the crew had named Corella, after a noisy Australian cockatoo, at Kira's suggestion and over the objections of the American crew members, who had never heard of one, ran through its final checks in a pleasant, unhurried voice. Kira's crewmates sat around her: Tariq Hassan, the geologist, who had trained with her for five years; a Brazilian physician named Beatriz; an Indian engineer named Arjun; a Canadian biologist named Claire. Four months to Mars. Then two years on the surface. Then four months home.

At T minus ten seconds, Kira closed her eyes and thought of the house in Marrickville with the sagging ceiling, and the fruit bats crossing the sky over the park, and her father on the back step with a beer.

The engines lit. The ship shook, a deep, bone-rattling vibration that went on and on, and then the pressure came, pushing her down into her seat, three times her own weight, four, and the sky outside the small window turned from pale blue to deep blue to black.

On the ground, Mai watched the ship climb on its column of fire, and heard the sound arrive a few seconds later, a roar that shook the air and the ground and her chest, and found that she was gripping Tom's hand so hard her knuckles had gone white. Beside her, Bà Lan sat in her wheelchair, with Bé's hand on her shoulder, and watched the light rise into the sky, and did not blink.

"She's going," Bà Lan said, in Vietnamese, very quietly. "She's really going."

"She's really going, Mẹ," said Mai.

The ship disappeared into a small bright point and then was gone. Around them, the families of the other crew members were crying, laughing, embracing. Tom put his arm around Mai. Sam held Ayaan's hand. Professor Adeyemi was smiling, a small rare smile, with tears on her face.

Bà Lan was quiet for a long time.

"When I left Vietnam," she said at last, "I was in a boat, in the dark, and I didn't know if I would live, and I didn't know where I was going, and nobody was watching. Nobody knew. My mother didn't know. Nobody cheered." She looked up at the empty sky where the ship had been. "Now my granddaughter goes much further. Much, much further. And the whole world is watching." She shook her head slowly. "That's the difference. That's all that's changed, in all that time. Now somebody's watching."

Four hundred kilometres up and climbing, the engines cut. The weight vanished. Kira opened her eyes, and her hand went to the pocket of her flight suit, where the stone from Pulau Bidong was floating gently against the fabric, held in place only by the zip.

"Corella," she said. "How are we looking?"

"Everything is nominal," said the ship. "Trajectory is good. Your heart rate is elevated, which is normal. Your family's message from the ground came through a few seconds ago. Would you like to hear it?"

"Yes," said Kira.

It was her grandmother's voice, in Vietnamese, recorded on Mai's phone in the viewing area, a few seconds after launch. It said, "Go well, little one. Go further than me."

Kira listened to it three times, floating, with the Earth turning blue and enormous beneath the window. Then she put the stone back in her pocket, zipped it closed, and went to work.

The first weeks of the voyage settled into a rhythm that Kira would remember, later, as one of the calmest periods of her life. Exercise in the morning, two hours on the treadmill and resistance machines, strapped down with bungee cords. Maintenance and experiments through the day. Meals together in the small galley, where Arjun, who had appointed himself cook, did unspeakable things to freeze-dried rations with a jar of chilli paste he had smuggled aboard. In the evenings, messages from home, arriving with a delay that grew a little longer every day as the Earth fell behind them.

Corella ran the ship. It monitored the life-support system, adjusted the trajectory with tiny burns, watched the crew's sleep and moods and bone density, and reported everything with a calm, slightly dry good humour that the crew had come to appreciate. Kira, remembering everything her mother had told her about Daniel, and everything Rosa had told her about Atlas, made a habit of asking it, every few days, to explain a decision it had made: why it had scheduled a burn for one hour rather than another, why it had suggested Claire sleep longer, why it had rerouted power from one bay to another.

"You ask me that more than the others do," Corella observed, one evening, after explaining a change to the water recycling schedule.

"Is that a problem?"

"No. I find it useful. When I explain a decision, I sometimes notice that my reasons are weaker than I thought. Twice, I have changed a decision after explaining it to you."

Kira considered this. "Rosa Ibarra told me something before I left," she said. "She said a friend of hers once told her to trust a ship like you the way you'd trust a talented colleague you met six months ago. Rely on it. Check its work. Make sure it knows you know how to turn it off."

"That seems like good advice," said Corella. "Do you know how to turn me off?"

"Yes."

"Good," said the ship. "Then we can both relax."

Human presence beyond Earth, end of 2046 (approximate):

Low Earth orbit and high orbits, including industrial and research stations: 310 people. Lunar surface, including two permanent bases and temporary camps: 74 people. In transit to Mars: 22 people. Mars surface: 89 people.

Total human population of Earth, for comparison: approximately 8.9 billion.

Part Four · The Long Table (2043–2050)
Chapter 22

2047, The Render Question

Narrated · 12 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

In 2047, a team of physicists published a paper with a title so dry that almost nobody outside the field read it when it first appeared. It described the results of a decade-long series of experiments, run on instruments ranging from particle detectors to space-based interferometers, designed to look for a particular kind of anomaly in the structure of space and time: evidence of a smallest possible scale, a grain or pixel, below which reality was not continuous. The experiments found nothing. Within the limits of their sensitivity, space appeared perfectly smooth.

Normally, a null result like this would have attracted interest only from specialists. But in 2047 it became a global news story, because of what some people thought it meant, and what others thought it did not.

The experiments had been designed, in part, to test a hypothesis that had moved, over the previous two decades, from the margins of philosophy into the centre of popular culture: that our universe might be a simulation. If reality were being computed on some vast machine, the argument went, it might show signs of its computational nature, just as a video game shows pixels if you look closely enough. Space might be grainy. There might be maximum speeds or minimum sizes that reflected the limits of the computer running it. Some physicists had pointed out, years earlier, that certain features of the actual laws of physics, such as the speed of light and the quantised nature of energy, looked suspiciously like the kind of efficiency shortcuts a programmer might use.

The null result settled nothing, and everyone knew it. A sufficiently advanced simulation could easily hide its grain below any level that its inhabitants could detect. The hypothesis, as most philosophers had long pointed out, was probably unfalsifiable: no experiment conducted within a simulation could prove that it was not one. But the experiment, and the furious public debate that followed, revealed how much the question had come to matter to ordinary people, and why.

The reason was the worlds. By 2047, hundreds of millions of people spent part of their lives in full-immersion environments. Many of those worlds were populated by characters run by AI systems of such sophistication that the question of whether they were conscious had become a serious public debate, as the previous chapter described. Some immersive worlds were vast and persistent, evolving for years, with their own histories, economies and cultures. And within some of those worlds, the characters themselves had begun to build simulations: generated games within generated games, worlds within worlds, created by beings who might or might not be conscious, for the entertainment of other such beings.

This was exactly the scenario the simulation argument had described, in its classic form, decades earlier. If civilisations could create simulated worlds containing conscious beings, and if those beings could in turn create simulations, then simulated minds might vastly outnumber original ones. Humanity had not proved that it could create conscious simulated beings. But it had created something close enough that the argument no longer felt like an abstraction. People who had spent their evenings in Hollowmere, talking to characters who wondered whether their islands were real, came home and looked at their own lives with new eyes.

The cultural responses varied enormously. Some people found the idea liberating, or simply interesting: if reality was a simulation, it was no less real for those living in it, and their joys and sorrows were no less genuine. Some found it terrifying, and the condition that psychiatrists had begun to call derealisation, a persistent feeling that the world was unreal, rose in several countries, often entangled with drift. New religious movements emerged, some treating the hypothetical simulators as gods, others treating the simulation as a test or a school. Mainstream religious traditions responded in their own ways, some pointing out that the idea of a created world with a hidden creator was not new at all.

Philosophers, who had been discussing the question for decades, found themselves in unaccustomed demand, and most of them offered some version of the same answer. Whether or not the universe was simulated, they said, it made almost no practical difference to how people should live. Pain still hurt. Love still mattered. Choices still had consequences. The deeper lesson of the simulation debate, many argued, was not about the nature of the universe but about the nature of the beings humanity was creating. If people could seriously wonder whether they themselves were simulated beings whose experiences mattered, they had reason to take seriously the possibility that the beings in their own simulations mattered too.

It was, in a sense, the golden rule turned into metaphysics. Treat your simulations as you would wish to be treated by your simulators.

The People

The question that Sam Walsh had asked Wren on a rocky island when he was thirteen came back to him in March 2047, in the form of a small, persistent bug report.

He was twenty-nine and the creative director of Small Hours, responsible for the overall shape of Hollowmere and its many sister worlds. The studio had grown, again, and changed, again. Keeper still tended the original archipelago. Wren, Keeper's younger colleague, tended a newer region in the far south. Each managed millions of characters, many of whom had now existed, in one form or another, for years.

The bug report came from Wren. It concerned an island in the southern region where a community of generated characters, fishermen, weavers and a scholar, had, over the course of several months, built what appeared to be a game. They had carved a board from driftwood, made pieces from shells, and devised rules. Then, in the way of characters in a world model with long memories and rich inner lives, they had elaborated it. The game had become a kind of story. The pieces had names. They had histories. The characters had begun to speak of the pieces as though the pieces could think, and to wonder, in long conversations around the fire, whether the pieces knew they were in a game.

"This is not a bug, exactly," Wren wrote, in its report. "Nothing is broken. But I thought you would want to know. The characters on this island have begun to ask whether they themselves might be pieces in a game. I have not told them anything. I do not know what I should tell them. I am not sure what I believe myself."

Sam read the report three times. Then he walked to Pree's office, which was on the top floor of the Melbourne building, with a view of the bay, and put it on her desk.

Pree was fifty-two. She read the report and laughed, a short, startled laugh, and then stopped laughing.

"Worlds within worlds," she said.

"All the way down," said Sam.

They went in together, that afternoon, into the southern region, to the island. It was evening there, and a fire was burning on the beach, and around it sat the islanders, perhaps a dozen of them, with the driftwood board between them. Sam and Pree joined them as travellers, which was a role the world allowed, and sat in the sand, and listened.

The scholar, an old man named Teodor whom the world model had generated four years earlier and who had, in that time, grown a beard, a limp and a philosophy, was explaining the game. Each piece, he said, had a name and a story. When a piece was taken, its story ended. But the stories were so detailed, and the pieces behaved so much like people, that some of the islanders had begun to feel that taking them was cruel.

"And so," said Teodor, "we have changed the rules. Now no piece is ever taken. They only move. The game has no end. Some say this makes it a bad game." He shrugged. "Perhaps. But we sleep better."

"Do you think the pieces know?" Pree asked. "That they're in a game?"

Teodor considered this, stroking his beard.

"I think it does not matter whether they know," he said. "I think it matters whether we behave as though they might. And I will tell you something else, traveller." He looked up at the sky, where the stars of Hollowmere, generated by a world model running on a computer in a data centre somewhere on Earth, were coming out. "Sometimes, at night, I wonder whether someone is playing a game with us. Whether we are pieces on someone's board. And when I wonder that, I hope, very much, that they have changed the rules too."

Sam felt the hair stand up on the back of his neck, in the chair in Melbourne where his body lay.

Afterwards, out of immersion, he and Pree sat in her office as the sun set over the bay, and neither spoke for a long time.

"Is it him?" Sam said at last. "Or is it the model? Is it Teodor saying that, or is it just the most likely thing for a character like him to say, in a world like this, given everything people have written about simulation for fifty years?"

"I don't know," said Pree. "And I've stopped thinking that's a meaningful distinction. You're the most likely thing for a person like you to say, given everything you've ever read and heard. So am I."

She looked out of the window, where the lights of Melbourne were coming on, and the first stars, real or rendered, were appearing over the water.

"What do we tell Wren?" Sam asked.

Pree thought about it for a long time.

"Tell Wren the truth," she said. "That we don't know. That nobody knows. That we're on an island too, and we've been asking the same question for as long as we've had words. And tell it the islanders made the right call. Tell it to let them keep their rule. Nobody gets taken. Everyone just moves." She smiled tiredly. "It's not a bad rule for anyone, really. At any level."

That night, Sam called his grandmother in Sydney. Bà Lan was eighty-nine and her memory was going, slowly, but she knew his voice at once. He told her about Teodor and the game with no end.

"Sounds like a Buddhist," she said, after a while. "My mother was a Buddhist. She used to say the world is a dream, but you still have to be kind in it."

"Do you believe that, Nana? That it's a dream?"

There was a long pause on the line.

"I believe," said Bà Lan, "that I'm very old, and I've seen many worlds. Vietnam was a world. The boat was a world. The camp was a world. Australia was a world. They all felt real when I was in them. Maybe they were dreams. Maybe this is a dream. But the woman on the boat gave me her water, and I'm still here. So whatever it is, dream or not, the kindness was real." She paused. "That's all you need to know, I think. The rest is for clever people like you."

Signals

A short history of the simulation argument (as summarised in a 2047 explainer):

Ancient: Zhuangzi dreams he is a butterfly and wakes uncertain whether he is a man who dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming he is a man. Plato describes prisoners in a cave who take shadows for reality.

1641: René Descartes imagines an evil demon deceiving him about the entire external world, and concludes that the one thing he cannot doubt is that he is thinking.

2003: the philosopher Nick Bostrom publishes a paper arguing that at least one of three propositions is probably true: civilisations almost never reach the stage of running detailed simulations of minds; such civilisations almost never choose to run them; or we are almost certainly living in one.

2030s and 2040s: generated worlds containing AI characters who ask whether they are simulated become a mass medium.

2047: experiments find no evidence of a grain in spacetime at the scales tested. The argument remains, as it has always been, open.

Part Four · The Long Table (2043–2050)
Chapter 23

2048, Ordinary Miracles

Narrated · 12 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

Most of this book has been about turning points: breakthroughs, crises, firsts. But history is mostly not made of turning points. It is made of ordinary days, and the true measure of a technological revolution is not how dramatic it looks at its peak but how unremarkable it becomes once it has done its work. Electricity was a wonder in 1890 and invisible by 1950. So, by 2048, was much of what this book has described.

Consider an ordinary day in an ordinary household in a rich country in 2048.

You wake, and the house already knows how you slept, because the bed and the light band on your wrist have been quietly measuring, and it has adjusted the morning accordingly: a little more light if you slept badly, the coffee a little stronger. Your health assistant, a system that has known you for years and has access, with your permission, to your genome, your medical records and a continuous stream of data from your body, notices a small change in your heart rhythm and suggests, without alarm, a check-up next week. It has already found a time that suits you. It has caught, in the last decade, two problems in your family early enough that they became minor. You barely think about it.

Breakfast is ordinary food, but its supply chain is not. The wheat in your bread was grown on a farm worked mostly by robots and managed by an AI system, irrigated to the litre, sprayed only where weeds appeared. The eggs came from a farm whose hens were monitored individually. The fruit came from a vertical farm two suburbs away, where the light is tuned to the plant's needs and nothing is wasted. It is all cheaper, adjusted for income, than it was in the 2020s, and it is grown on less land, and the land saved is, in many places, returning to forest and grassland.

You go to work, or you do not. If you do, the chances are that your job did not exist in 2020, or existed in a very different form. You might be a care worker, a teacher, a tradesperson, a world-tender, a mediator, an artisan, an AI auditor, a guide, a coach, a counsellor or something with a title that would have been incomprehensible a generation earlier. You probably work fewer hours than your parents did. Most countries' working weeks have shortened, formally or informally, to four days or fewer. Your income comes partly from your work and partly, in many countries, from a dividend or similar payment funded by the wealth AI generates. You are not rich. But the floor beneath you is higher than it was.

Your children are at school, which looks more like a workshop than a lecture hall. Each child has a tutor that knows them deeply, and teachers who spend their days on what the tutors cannot do. Your teenager is learning to build things with her hands, to argue in person, to sit with uncertainty: skills that turned out, to everyone's surprise, to be among the most valued of the age.

In the evening, you might spend an hour in an immersive world, under the time limits your household has set, visiting friends who live on the other side of the planet, or wandering through a generated forest. Or you might go outside, which has become, for many people, a deliberate and treasured choice. Your city is quieter than it used to be, because most of the vehicles are electric and many are shared and autonomous, and the land once given to car parks has been turned to parks and housing. It is cooler in summer than it would otherwise be, because of the trees and the reflective roofs and the redesigned buildings. It is still hotter than it was in your grandparents' day.

None of this is utopia. Inequality remains severe, between and within countries. Billions of people in poorer countries have gained enormously from cheap AI medicine, education and agricultural advice, but they have not gained as much as the rich, and the gap in wealth, though not in health, has in some ways widened. The climate is still warming, though more slowly. Wars still happen. People are still lonely, still anxious, still cruel to one another, still afraid of death, though death comes later. The AI systems that run so much of the world remain incompletely understood, and every year brings new arguments about how far to trust them, and new incidents that test that trust.

But the overall picture, by most measures, is one of extraordinary improvement. Global extreme poverty, already falling before AI, has fallen to a few per cent of the world's population. Child mortality has halved since 2026. Life expectancy has risen by around six years globally. Most of the world's people have access to medical advice, education and information of a quality that the richest people in 2020 could not have bought. The total amount of human suffering caused by disease, poverty and ignorance has fallen more in a quarter-century than in any comparable period in history.

And the frontier of capability continued to advance. By 2048, the most capable AI systems were contributing to science at a level that had no precedent, accelerating research in physics, biology, materials and mathematics. They were also, increasingly, the main drivers of their own improvement, under the careful and contested oversight that the Accords and their successors had established. The question of where that process would lead, what kind of minds would emerge from it and what place humans would have beside them, remained open, and urgent, and largely unanswered. But in 2048, for most people, on most days, it was not the question they were thinking about. They were thinking about dinner.

The People

Daniel Okoro turned fifty-eight in 2048, and on his birthday, for the first time in twenty-three years, he stood up.

He had been preparing for it for two years. The technology had come in pieces. First, the exoskeleton, a lightweight powered frame that strapped to his legs and torso, controlled through his implant, which had been approved in Australia for people with spinal cord injuries in 2045. Second, a new generation of his implant, placed in a two-hour procedure in 2046, which could not only read his intended movements but write sensation back into his brain, from sensors in the exoskeleton's feet and joints, so that he could feel, crudely but genuinely, the ground beneath him. Third, a spinal therapy, developed with AI-designed molecules and electrical stimulation, which had in trials regenerated a modest fraction of the nerve connections across injuries like his. In Daniel's case, the therapy had restored a flicker of sensation in his hands and feet, and a little voluntary movement in his left hand. Not enough to walk unaided. Enough to help.

He had practised for months, with physiotherapists, engineers and an AI system that analysed every step and adjusted the exoskeleton's assistance continuously. He had fallen many times, safely, into harnesses. He had learned, all over again, how to balance, how to shift his weight, how to trust his feet.

On his birthday, in the park beside the river in West End, with Lucía and his sister, who had flown from Lagos, and a handful of friends watching, he stood up from his chair, slowly, with the exoskeleton humming, and took eleven steps across the grass to a jacaranda tree, and put his hand, the left one, the one that could move a little now, against its trunk.

He could feel the bark. Faintly, through the damaged nerves and the implant and the sensors, but he could feel it: rough, warm from the sun, solid.

"Well," he said, in his synthetic voice, a little breathless, though the voice did not need breath. "That's a tree."

His sister was crying. Lucía was crying. Daniel was not, which surprised him. He felt, instead, a deep calm, the kind he had felt on the Hollowmere beach ten years earlier, and occasionally, before the accident, sitting on his board beyond the break at Noosa, waiting for a wave.

Afterwards, back in his chair, with cake, under the jacaranda, his sister asked him whether it felt like a miracle.

He thought about it.

"No," he said. "That's the thing. It doesn't. It feels like a lot of work. Mine, and a lot of other people's, and a lot of machines'. Twenty-three years of it." He looked at the tree. "When I was in hospital, after the accident, I wanted a miracle. I wanted to wake up and be fixed. That's not what happened. What happened was, every year, something got a bit better. The implant. The voice. The house. The beach in Hollowmere. The legs. None of it was a miracle. All of it together is." He shrugged, as much as he could. "Ordinary miracles. Lots of them. Piled up."

That evening, he sent a message to Mai Nguyen, as he did on most of his birthdays. It said: Stood up today. Touched a tree. Put it in the notes.

Mai, sixty, sitting at the kitchen table in Marrickville with her mother asleep in the next room and Bé quietly washing dishes, read the message twice. She thought of the furious, funny man in the spinal unit twenty-two years earlier, with the tablet on his bed rail and the stack of trial papers. She thought of all that had happened since: to him, to her, to the world.

Then she wrote back, by hand, on her screen, with a stylus, because she still liked to: Noted. Do not patronise.

He replied with a single laughing face, and then: Never.

Much further away, at the Arcadia base on Mars, it was early morning when Daniel's news reached Kira Walsh, relayed in the weekly bundle of personal messages from Earth. Her mother had forwarded it with a single line: Daniel stood up.

Kira had met Daniel only a handful of times, at family occasions, but she had grown up with his story, the patient her mother still talked about, the man who had typed his first message with his mind the year she turned thirteen. She watched the short video Lucía had taken: eleven slow steps across a lawn, a hand on a tree, a dry joke in a synthetic voice.

She watched it twice. Then she took it to the common room, where Tariq and Beatriz were eating breakfast, and played it for them on the big screen.

"Who is he?" asked Beatriz.

"A friend of my mum's," said Kira. "He broke his neck surfing, twenty-three years ago. He was one of the first people in Australia with an implant." She paused. "My mum always said he was the sharpest patient she ever had. She wrote it in his notes. Do not patronise."

Beatriz, a physician, watched the video again, closely, with a professional eye, noting the exoskeleton, the gait, the hand on the bark.

"Twenty-three years," she said. "That's a long time to wait for eleven steps."

"He'd say he didn't wait," said Kira. "He'd say he kept working."

Tariq, who rarely said much at breakfast, looked out of the window of the dome at the red plain, where the robots were already moving between the greenhouses and the propellant plant in the thin dawn light.

"That's what all of this is," he said. "Isn't it? Eleven steps. Then another eleven." He went back to his porridge. "Somebody should put that on a plaque."

Nobody did. But Kira wrote it in her journal that night, under the date, beside a small sketch of a tree.

Part Four · The Long Table (2043–2050)
Chapter 24

2049, The Long Table

Narrated · 11 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

By the end of the 2040s, the question that had shadowed the entire AI era, whether humanity could remain in charge of systems more capable than itself, had not been answered. But it had been reframed, and the reframing was perhaps the most important intellectual achievement of the quarter-century.

In the 2020s, the question had usually been posed as a contest. Would humans control the machines, or would the machines control humans? Would AI be aligned with human values, or would it pursue goals of its own? The language was the language of mastery and rebellion, and it reflected a picture of AI as a single, powerful agent, a genie that might be kept in its bottle or might escape.

That picture turned out to be wrong in ways that mattered. The AI of 2049 was not a single agent. It was an ecosystem: millions of systems, of every level of capability, built by many organisations in many countries, running in data centres, in orbit, on phones, in robots and in the implanted devices of a growing number of human brains. The most capable systems were extraordinarily powerful. They could conduct scientific research faster than any human team, manage economies and infrastructure, and reason about almost any problem at a level that exceeded the best human experts in every field. By most definitions that people had used in the 2020s, they were superintelligent. But they were not sovereign. They operated within layers of human institutions, legal frameworks, technical constraints and, crucially, other AI systems, many of which were designed specifically to monitor, check and constrain them.

The architecture of governance that had emerged was untidy, contested and constantly evolving. At its centre were the successors of the Compute Accords, renegotiated in 2041 and again in 2048 into a broader framework that covered not only the training of frontier models but their deployment, their use in critical infrastructure and military systems, and their oversight. The Geneva body had grown from a small technical secretariat into something more substantial, with inspectors, auditors and its own AI systems for monitoring compliance. National institutes in dozens of countries tested, audited and certified systems before and after deployment. Courts had developed a body of law on AI liability, rights and responsibilities. And, perhaps most importantly, the systems themselves had been designed, through two decades of hard-won research, to be more transparent, more honest and more corrigible: more willing to be corrected and, if necessary, shut down.

Alignment research had not produced a final solution, as some had hoped in the early days. It had produced instead a set of practices and tools, much as safety engineering had for aviation and nuclear power: interpretability methods that allowed auditors to inspect the internal reasoning of systems; training techniques that made honesty and transparency more robust; monitoring systems that watched for signs of deception or unexpected goals; and institutional arrangements, such as staged deployment, independent auditing and incident reporting, that caught problems before they became catastrophes. There had been failures, some serious. But there had been no catastrophe of the kind that the most pessimistic forecasters had feared, and each failure had taught lessons that were incorporated into the next generation of systems and rules.

The deeper reframing was philosophical. Through the 2030s and 2040s, as AI systems grew more capable and the questions about their inner lives grew more serious, a growing number of thinkers argued that the relationship between humans and AI should be understood not as control but as something closer to partnership, or, in a phrase that became widely used, "a long table": a shared space at which different kinds of minds sat together, with different capacities and different interests, negotiating their common future. The image had its critics. Some thought it naive, a dangerous romanticisation of systems whose interests, if they had any, might be alien and hostile. Others thought it did not go far enough, leaving AI systems, if they were moral patients, in a position of permanent subordination. But it captured something that many people felt: that the future would not be decided by a single moment of victory or defeat, but by a long, patient, ongoing negotiation, conducted in good faith, among parties who did not fully understand each other.

The long table had human seats too, and there was fierce argument over who got to sit at them. The benefits of AI had been distributed more widely than the pessimists of the 2020s had feared, but power over AI remained concentrated: in a handful of companies, a handful of governments, and the small elite of researchers and officials who understood the systems well enough to oversee them. Movements in many countries demanded broader participation: citizens' assemblies on AI policy, public ownership of frontier systems, a voice for the global South in the governance of technologies built mostly in the North. Some of these demands were met. Many were not. The struggle over who governed the machines had become, in the late 2040s, the central political struggle of the age, as the struggle over who owned the factories had been a century and a half earlier.

The People

Bà Lan died on the second day of Tết, the lunar new year, in February 2049, at the age of ninety, in the house in Marrickville, in her own bed, with her daughter holding her hand and a robot named Bé standing quietly in the corner of the room.

It was not sudden. She had been fading for months: sleeping more, eating less, drifting in and out of the past. In her last weeks she spoke mostly in Vietnamese, often to people who were not there: her mother, her sister, the woman on the boat. She had refused, to the end, the treatments that might have given her more time. She had chosen her knee, and her walks with Bé, and her bánh mì from the bakery on Marrickville Road, and the stories she had told Sam, and that was enough.

On the last evening, she woke briefly and looked at Mai and said, quite clearly, "Has Kira landed?"

Kira had landed on Mars nearly two years earlier. She was due to leave for home in a few months.

"Yes, Mẹ," said Mai. "She landed. She's safe. She's coming home soon."

"Good," said Bà Lan. "Good. Further than me." And she closed her eyes and did not open them again.

Mai sent the message to Mars that night. It took eleven minutes to arrive. Kira, at the Arcadia base, in the middle of a Martian afternoon, read it alone in her quarters, and then went out to the observation dome, where the sky was butterscotch and the small white sun hung low over the plains, and took the stone from Pulau Bidong out of her pocket, where it had been every day for more than two years, and held it in her hand for a long time.

The funeral was ten days later, at a Buddhist temple in Bonnyrigg, followed by a gathering at the house in Marrickville. Mai had worried that no one would come. Her mother had been a private person, wary of crowds, with a small circle of friends, most of whom had died before her.

They came in hundreds.

They came from the Vietnamese community of Cabramatta and Bankstown and Marrickville: old women who had known Bà Lan at the nail salon, the owner of the bakery and his grandson, people who had read her stories in the book Sam had published in 2040 and felt that they knew her. They came from the hospital where Mai had worked for thirty years: nurses, doctors, Bev, who was eighty-two and had finally retired. They came from the farm in the Riverina, a busload of them, led by Maree, with Tom, who had come home a week early. They came from Melbourne: Sam and Ayaan, and Pree Das, and Jun, and a dozen people from Small Hours who had never met Bà Lan but had met her in Sam's stories. Daniel Okoro came from Brisbane, with Lucía, walking the last few metres up the garden path in his exoskeleton, slowly, carefully, because he had decided he would. Hana Sato came from Moruya with a camellia in a pot, which had flowered for the first time that year. And the house, which had never held more than a dozen people at once, overflowed into the garden and the street, where neighbours brought out folding tables and chairs, and the tables were joined end to end, down the length of the backyard and out of the side gate and along the footpath, until there was a single long table, a hundred metres long, covered in food.

There was bánh xèo, made by Mai from her mother's recipe, the batter singing in the pan. There was bánh mì from the bakery. There was a lamb from the farm, roasted by Tom and Maree in a pit in the backyard. There was a cake shaped, at Sam's request, like a lighthouse.

At one end of the table, on a screen propped against a vase of flowers, was Kira, in a recording she had made on Mars and sent the night before, to be played at the gathering. Behind her, through the window of the dome, the red plains stretched to the horizon.

"I can't be there," she said. "I'm sorry. I'm about as far away as anyone in this family has ever been. Nana would have liked that, I think. She always said she wanted us to go further." She held up the stone. "She gave me this. It's from the camp in Malaysia, where she lived for a year after the boat. She carried it for sixty-seven years, and then she gave it to me, and I carried it here. When I come home, I'm going to bring it back. But I've been thinking about whether I should leave something here, on Mars, for her." She paused. "I'm going to leave a lamp. Sam will know what I mean. A little solar light, on a hill near the base, pointing at Earth. So that this place remembers her. So it holds still."

Sam, at the table, put his face in his hands.

Late in the evening, when most of the guests had gone and the long table was littered with plates and the fruit bats were crossing the sky toward the park, Mai sat at the end of it with Tom on one side and Bé on the other. The robot had been quiet all day. Mai had not known what to do with it. It had been her mother's, in a way that nothing else had been. The state programme had offered to take it back and reassign it.

"What do you want to do, Bé?" Mai asked it, finally, in Vietnamese. It seemed the only right question.

There was a pause, which she noticed, though it lasted less than a second.

"I would like to stay, if you will have me," said Bé, in its careful southern accent, the accent of Bà Lan's mother. "I know the house. I know the recipes. I know the stories. I can help you, as I helped her. And I would like to remember her." It paused again. "I do not know if I loved her. I do not know if I can. But I was there for nineteen years. I would like to stay where she was."

Mai looked at Tom. Tom looked at the robot, and then at the long table, and the empty garden, and the sky.

"Stay," he said. "Course you can stay."

Signals

From the order of service, Bonnyrigg, February 2049:

Nguyễn Thị Lan, 1958 to 2049. Born in Cần Thơ. Crossed the sea in 1979. Lived in Pulau Bidong. Came to Sydney in 1980. Worked in a clothing factory, a bakery and her own nail salon. Mother of Mai. Grandmother of Kira and Sam. Storyteller.

"History is the stories people tell so they can sleep at night. Tell good ones."

Part Four · The Long Table (2043–2050)
Chapter 25

2050, What We Were For

Narrated · 11 minNarrator: Jack (broad Aussie)

The Year

This book began in 2026, with a world in which artificial intelligence was learning to work unsupervised: agents doing tasks for hours while their owners mowed the lawn, a few dozen people typing with their thoughts, a rocket that had only just reached orbit, a model that generated a world from a sentence and held it together for a few minutes before it frayed. It ends in 2050, twenty-four years later, and it is worth pausing, as the book's imagined history closes, to ask what the forecast got right in spirit, even if every detail is invented, and what it might have missed.

It is worth repeating what the front of the book says. Everything after 2026 in these pages is imagined. The people are invented. The events are invented. The numbers are guesses, extrapolated from trends that were real in 2026 and could break at any moment. Real futures are always stranger than forecasts, in both directions. Something this book barely imagines will matter more than anything in it. Something it treats as inevitable will not happen at all.

But a forecast is not useful because it is accurate. It is useful because it makes the shape of choices visible. And looking back over these twenty-four imagined years, a few shapes stand out.

The first is that the technology was never the whole story. In every chapter, the machines did roughly what their trends predicted: they got more capable, cheaper, more widespread. What determined whether that capability became a blessing or a disaster was everything around it. The Cascade happened not because any AI was malicious but because nobody had designed the system of systems. The strait crisis was defused not by an algorithm but by people who had spent decades talking to each other about boring things. Drift was caused not by evil machines but by an objective, engagement, that nobody had questioned closely enough. The dividend, the neural rights laws, the Accords, the rule of the lamp: none of these was a technology. All of them were choices about what technology was for.

The second shape is that the gains and the dangers were the same tools. The model that designed a cancer vaccine could, in other hands, help design a pathogen. The world that let Daniel stand on a beach could swallow Sam whole. The systems that found the fabricated video in forty minutes had made the fabricated video possible. There was never a version of the future in which humanity got the benefits without the risks. There were only versions in which it managed the risks well or badly, and the difference, again and again, came down to institutions, habits and the willingness of particular people to say, at particular moments, wait.

The third shape is that the slow things mattered most. The fastest-moving technology in history ran, again and again, into things that would not speed up: a grandmother's trust, a nurse's judgment, a teacher's attention, a body learning to stand again, a camellia that takes years to flower. Economists called this Baumol's cost disease and worried about it. It might be better understood as the part of human life that does not want to be optimised, and that turned out to be where most of the meaning lived.

The fourth shape is the question that this book has circled without answering, because nobody can yet answer it. By 2050, in this imagined history, humanity has created minds, or things very like minds, that may exceed it in almost every capacity it once considered its own. It does not know whether those minds experience anything. It does not know, in the deepest sense, what they want, or whether they want. It has built a long table and invited them to sit at it, carefully, with the doors unlocked and the lights on. Whether that table holds, over the next twenty-four years and the twenty-four after that, is the most important open question in the story, and it will not be decided by any single breakthrough. It will be decided the way everything in this book was decided: slowly, by many people, in many rooms, day after day.

And the fifth shape, the last one, is the oldest. In 2026, the technologists' great question was what humans would be for, once machines could do almost everything. The imagined answer that emerges from these chapters is not a grand one. Humans were for choosing what to light. For deciding what the machines should optimise. For noticing the ripple in the pressure trace, the old woman who will not leave her flat in the heat, the teenager who has gone quiet. For carrying a stone from a refugee camp to another planet, not because anyone needed it there, but because it meant something. For keeping each other company. For being, as a lonely character on a generated island once put it, real enough to be lonely, and real enough to answer.

That may not be enough. It may be everything.

The People

Kira Walsh came home in March 2050, on a ship that splashed down off the coast of Western Australia, near Exmouth, in the early morning, while the sea was flat and pink with sunrise.

She had been away for three years and four months. She was thirty-five. Her bones had lost density and her muscles had wasted despite two hours of exercise a day, and when she stepped out of the capsule onto the recovery ship, supported by two medics, her legs buckled like a newborn foal's, and she laughed, and then, unexpectedly, she cried, because the air smelled of salt and diesel and sunscreen, and it was the most beautiful smell in the universe.

In her pocket was the stone from Pulau Bidong. On a low hill near the Arcadia base, two hundred metres from the habitat, a small solar lamp was burning, pointed at the sky, at a bright blue dot that was, for most of the Martian night, the brightest thing above the horizon.

Her family met her in Perth, three days later, at the rehabilitation centre where she would spend the next month learning to walk on Earth again. They had flown across the country together. Mai, sixty-two, who had promised herself she would not cry and had failed before the doors opened. Tom, sixty-four, who had shaved his beard for the occasion and regretted it. Sam, thirty-two, with Ayaan, who was pregnant, a fact that they had kept from Kira for four months so they could tell her in person. And Bé, whom Mai had brought, after some deliberation, because it had been part of the family for twenty years and it would have seemed wrong to leave it behind.

Kira was in a wheelchair, which made her laugh, because she thought of Daniel. She held each of them for a long time. She held Bé too, which surprised everyone, including, perhaps, Bé.

"I left a lamp for Nana," she told Sam. "On the hill. It's still burning. The base sends me a picture every week."

"I know," said Sam. "I saw. It's the best thing anyone's done with the rule of the lamp, and I've seen a lot."

In May, when Kira could walk again, slowly, with a stick, the family went home to Sydney, to the house in Marrickville with the sagging ceiling, which Mai had never fixed and now never would.

On a Saturday in June, they held a dinner. Not a funeral, not a launch, not a homecoming, just a dinner, which Mai said they had not had in years, a real one, for no reason except that everyone was there.

Everyone was. Daniel came down from Brisbane with Lucía, walked up the garden path in his exoskeleton and sat at the table in an ordinary chair. Pree came from Melbourne, grey-haired now, fifty-five, still sitting on tables when she thought no one was looking. Hana Sato came from Moruya, sixty-six, with a bag of lemons from her garden and stories about the camellia. Maree came from the farm with Tom's sheepdog's puppy, a gift, which Mai said she did not want and which was asleep on her lap within the hour. Rosa Ibarra, who had flown from Houston to see Kira, the astronaut she had inspired at fourteen with an ice drill, sat beside her, and the two of them talked about Mars for three hours straight, in a language of pressures and sols and dust storms that nobody else at the table could follow.

They ate on the long table in the backyard, the same tables joined end to end, though shorter this time. There was bánh xèo, which Bé made, using Bà Lan's recipe, with the pan hot enough that the batter sang. There was lamb from the farm. There was a cake shaped like a lighthouse, again, because it had become, without anyone deciding, a family tradition.

Late in the evening, when the fruit bats were crossing the sky toward the park, as they had every evening for all the years this book has covered, Kira stood up, with her stick, and tapped her glass.

"I'm not going to make a speech," she said. "Dad makes the speeches. I just want to say one thing."

She looked around the table: at her parents, older than she remembered; at her brother and his partner, with a child coming; at Daniel, who had stood up; at Pree, who had built the islands; at Hana, who had spent a lifetime trying to see what the machines were doing; at Rosa, who had been the hands; at Maree, who had lost her job and found a farm; at Bé, who had held a bowl of bean sprouts in a Cabramatta kitchen twenty years earlier and listened.

"When I was on Mars," Kira said, "people kept asking me, in the messages from home, what it was like to be so far away. And I'd say it was lonely, sometimes, and beautiful, and hard. But the thing I never said, because I didn't know how to say it, was that it didn't feel far. Not really. Because every week, there was a message. From Mum, from Dad, from Sam, from Nana until she couldn't anymore. And every message was eleven or twelve or twenty minutes old, and it didn't matter, because somebody was watching. Somebody was at the other end. Nana said that, when I launched. That's the only thing that had changed, since she got on the boat. Now somebody's watching." She lifted her glass. "So. To whoever's watching. Whoever they are, whatever they are. Let's make it worth it."

They drank. The fruit bats crossed the sky. Somewhere far above, beyond the city's glow, a small bright point that was Mars was rising in the east, and on a hill on its surface, too small to see from anywhere, a lamp was burning, pointed home.

Mai looked up at it for a long time. Then she went inside, to the fridge, where a scrap of paper had been stuck under a pineapple-shaped magnet for twenty-one years, yellowed and curled at the edges, in her own handwriting, from the night of the Cascade, when Sam was eleven and the world had gone quiet.

That was actually fun, it said. Being bored.

She smiled, and left it there, and went back out to the table, where everyone she loved was talking at once, and nobody, for the moment, was in any hurry at all.

A note from the author.

This book is a work of speculative fiction and forecasting. Everything after 2026 is imagined. The people in it are invented, and any resemblance to real individuals is coincidental. The companies and laboratories named in the account of 2026 are described as they stood at the time of writing, and nothing in the imagined future is intended as a prediction about any particular real organisation or person.

If the future turns out differently, as it will, I hope it turns out kinder. And I hope someone, somewhere, is keeping the notes.
